67	**3.2** The Government agrees to defer prosecution of the Criminal Information for the duration of the Term, provided that Greenvale fully and timely complies with all terms and conditions of this Agreement. The Government shall seek the consent of the Court, pursuant to Title 18, United States Code, Section 3161(h)(2), to the exclusion of time under the Speedy Trial Act for the duration of the Term of this Agreement.
68	
69	**3.3** Upon successful completion of all terms and conditions of this Agreement, including but not limited to the payment of all monetary penalties and civil settlement amounts, the fulfillment of all cooperation obligations, the satisfaction of all compliance program enhancement requirements, and the satisfactory conclusion of the Independent Compliance Monitor\'s mandate, the Government shall, within thirty (30) days of the expiration of the Term, move to dismiss the Criminal Information with prejudice.
70	
71	**3.4** In the event that the Government determines that Greenvale has breached any provision of this Agreement, the Government may proceed with prosecution as set forth in Section 12 of this Agreement. Nothing in this Section 3 shall limit the Government\'s rights or remedies under Section 12 of this Agreement.
72	
73	**3.5** The Government may, in its sole discretion, extend the Term of this Agreement for an additional period of up to one (1) year upon written notice to the Company, provided that such extension is based upon a good-faith determination that additional time is reasonably necessary for the Company to fulfill its obligations hereunder or for the Independent Compliance Monitor to complete its work.
74	
75	**[SECTION 4 --- RELEVANT CONDUCT]{.underline}**
76	
77	**4.1 Speaker Programs.** During the Relevant Period (January 1, 2019 through December 31, 2022), Greenvale operated nationwide speaker programs for its branded pharmaceutical products Neurovan and Cardivex. These speaker programs were managed by the Company\'s commercial organization, specifically its sales and marketing divisions, with oversight from the Medical Affairs department. Over the four-year Relevant Period, Greenvale conducted approximately 4,200 speaker events per year, for a total of approximately 16,800 speaker events. Total speaker honoraria paid by the Company during the Relevant Period amounted to approximately \$38.6 million, allocated as follows: \$8.4 million in fiscal year 2019; \$10.2 million in fiscal year 2020; \$11.1 million in fiscal year 2021; and \$8.9 million in fiscal year 2022.
78	
79	The Government alleges that approximately 1,150 of these speaker events across the four-year Relevant Period were \"sham\" programs that did not serve a legitimate medical education purpose. In these sham events, one or more of the following conditions was present: (a) the engaged speaker did not deliver a genuine medical education presentation consistent with the approved slide deck or educational materials; (b) the audience consisted primarily or exclusively of the speaker\'s own office staff, who had no prescribing authority and no legitimate need for the information presented; or (c) the event was held at a high-end restaurant with food and beverage expenditures exceeding any reasonable educational purpose, and no meaningful educational content was delivered. The Government alleges that approximately \$14,300,000 in speaker honoraria was paid in connection with these sham events during the Relevant Period.
80	
81	**4.2 Consulting Arrangements.** During the Relevant Period, Greenvale maintained consulting arrangements with approximately 47 high-prescribing healthcare providers. These consulting arrangements took the form of advisory board participation, market research engagements, and clinical input agreements. Total consulting fees paid to these 47 healthcare providers during the Relevant Period amounted to approximately \$6.2 million, allocated as follows: \$1.1 million in fiscal year 2019; \$1.6 million in fiscal year 2020; \$1.9 million in fiscal year 2021; and \$1.6 million in fiscal year 2022. The Government alleges that these consulting fees were disproportionate to the services actually rendered by the healthcare providers and were intended as inducements to prescribe or continue prescribing Neurovan and Cardivex to patients, including patients enrolled in federal healthcare programs.
82	
83	**4.3 Total Alleged Improper Payments.** The total alleged improper payments during the Relevant Period amount to \$20,500,000, consisting of \$14,300,000 in improper speaker honoraria (as described in Section 4.1) and \$6,200,000 in improper consulting fees (as described in Section 4.2).
84	
85	**4.4 Statutory Violations.** The conduct described in Sections 4.1 through 4.3 constitutes violations of the Anti-Kickback Statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b, which prohibits the knowing and willful payment of remuneration to induce or reward referrals of items or services payable by federal healthcare programs. The improper payments described herein caused healthcare providers to prescribe Neurovan and Cardivex to patients enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and other federal healthcare programs, resulting in the submission of false or fraudulent claims for reimbursement in violation of the False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 *et seq.*
86	
87	**4.5 Named Individuals.** The Government\'s investigation identified the following individuals as having played significant roles in the conduct described in this Agreement: (a) Kevin Driscoll, Regional Sales Director, Northeast Region, who supervised sales representatives and district managers responsible for the recruitment and management of speaker program participants in the northeastern United States; (b) Maria Santos, Regional Sales Director, Southeast Region, who supervised sales representatives and district managers responsible for the recruitment and management of speaker program participants in the southeastern United States; and (c) Dr. Leonard Kwan, former Vice President of Medical Affairs, who departed Greenvale in March 2022 and who approved consulting fee arrangements and provided oversight of the speaker program from a medical affairs perspective. The Government\'s investigation is ongoing with respect to the conduct of these and other individuals.
88	
89	**4.6 Compliance Deficiencies.** During the Relevant Period, Greenvale\'s compliance infrastructure suffered from significant structural deficiencies. The Company\'s Chief Compliance Officer, Patricia Knowles, reported to the General Counsel, Janet Huang, rather than reporting directly to the Board of Directors\' Audit Committee, thereby compromising the independence of the compliance function. The compliance department\'s annual operating budget was reduced by approximately 18%, from \$4.8 million in fiscal year 2019 to \$3.936 million in fiscal year 2020, during a period when speaker program activity was expanding in both scope and expenditure. Between 2019 and 2022, the compliance department flagged 312 speaker events as potentially problematic based on internal monitoring criteria. Of those 312 flagged events, only 41 were actually cancelled; the remaining 271 events proceeded after what the Government characterizes as cursory review that did not adequately address the identified concerns.
90	
91	**[SECTION 5 --- ACCEPTANCE OF RESPONSIBILITY]{.underline}**
92	
93	**5.1** Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. accepts and acknowledges responsibility for the conduct set forth in this Agreement and in the Stipulated Statement of Facts attached hereto as Exhibit A. The Company recognizes and acknowledges that its conduct during the Relevant Period violated federal law, including the Anti-Kickback Statute and the False Claims Act, and that such conduct caused harm to the United States and to the integrity of federal healthcare programs.
94	
95	**5.2** Greenvale agrees that the facts set forth in Exhibit A are true and accurate and that Exhibit A provides a fair and accurate description of the Company\'s conduct during the Relevant Period. The Company further agrees that it will not dispute or contest the facts set forth in Exhibit A in any proceeding before any court, agency, or tribunal.
96	
97	**5.3** Greenvale agrees that it will not, through its attorneys, board members, agents, officers, employees, or any person authorized to speak on its behalf, make any public statement contradicting the acceptance of responsibility set forth in this Section 5 or the facts set forth in Exhibit A. Any such contradictory public statement by any person described in the preceding sentence, after consultation and authorization by the Company\'s senior management, shall constitute a breach of this Agreement as set forth in Section 12.
98	
99	**5.4** The Company voluntarily and knowingly waives any and all defenses based upon the statute of limitations for any prosecution that is or may be brought by the Government arising from or relating to the conduct described in this Agreement and the Stipulated Statement of Facts, for the duration of the Term plus one (1) year following the expiration or termination of this Agreement.
100	
101	**[SECTION 6 --- COOPERATION OBLIGATIONS]{.underline}**
102	
103	**[6.1 General Cooperation]{.underline}**
104	
105	Greenvale shall provide complete, truthful, and candid cooperation with the United States Attorney\'s Office for the District of New Jersey, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (\"FBI\"), the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (\"HHS-OIG\"), and any other federal, state, or local law enforcement agency involved in the investigation of the matters described in this Agreement or any related investigation. Such cooperation shall include, but not be limited to, truthful disclosure of all factual information not protected by a valid, applicable legal privilege, identification of witnesses, production of documents and records, and making employees and agents available for interviews, testimony, and other proceedings. The obligation to cooperate shall continue throughout the Term of this Agreement and shall extend to any matter related to or arising from the conduct described herein, including any investigation or prosecution of individuals.
106	
107	**[6.2 Document Production]{.underline}**
108	
109	Greenvale shall produce all documents, records, data, communications, and other materials requested by the Government in connection with the Government\'s investigation or any related investigation or proceeding, without assertion of any claim of privilege, including but not limited to attorney-client privilege, and any other applicable privilege or protection, **with the sole exception of** attorney-client privileged communications between Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and the law firm of Whitfield & Crane LLP, 1700 Market Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19103, made on or after June 15, 2021. All other documents, records, data, communications, and materials, including without limitation: (a) documents and communications predating June 15, 2021, regardless of whether such documents involve communications with Whitfield & Crane LLP or any other counsel; (b) documents and communications involving any counsel or law firm other than Whitfield & Crane LLP, regardless of when such documents were created; and (c) all materials not covered by the attorney-client privilege, including but not limited to documents and materials that may be subject to the work product doctrine, the joint defense privilege, or any other protection or immunity from disclosure, shall be produced upon request without objection. The Company acknowledges that this provision constitutes a voluntary waiver of any applicable privilege or protection, except as specifically and expressly limited above, and agrees that such waiver is knowing and voluntary.
110	
111	Documents shall be produced in the format requested by the Government, including in native electronic format where applicable. The Company shall produce documents within fourteen (14) business days of receipt of a written request from the Government, unless a different timeframe is agreed upon by the parties.
112	
113	**[6.3 Employee Availability]{.underline}**
114	
115	Greenvale shall use its best efforts to make available for interviews, testimony, depositions, grand jury proceedings, trial, or any other legal proceedings, any current or former officer, director, employee, agent, or consultant of the Company, as requested by the Government. Such availability shall include making employees available at the Government\'s offices in Newark, New Jersey, or at such other location as the Government may designate, at times reasonably convenient to the Government. The Company shall not discourage, directly or indirectly, any current or former employee from cooperating with the Government\'s investigation, and shall not instruct or advise any current or former employee to withhold information from the Government.
116	
117	**[6.4 Self-Reporting of New Violations]{.underline}**
118	
119	Greenvale shall report to the United States Attorney\'s Office for the District of New Jersey any new potential violation of federal criminal law or the Anti-Kickback Statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b, by the Company or any of its officers, directors, employees, or agents within seventy-two (72) hours of the Company\'s becoming aware of such potential violation. Such reports shall be made in writing, addressed to AUSA Patricia Moreno and AUSA David Kesselman, with copies to the Independent Compliance Monitor appointed pursuant to Section 9 of this Agreement. For purposes of this Section 6.4, the Company shall be deemed to be \"aware\" of a potential violation when any member of the Company\'s legal, compliance, or executive management team receives information that would cause a reasonable compliance professional to believe that a potential violation may have occurred. The self-reporting obligation set forth in this Section 6.4 shall apply regardless of whether the Company has completed any internal assessment or investigation of the potential violation and regardless of whether the Company has concluded that a violation has in fact occurred.
120	
121	**[6.5 Preservation Obligations]{.underline}**
122	
123	Greenvale shall preserve all documents, communications, records, data, and other materials relating to the conduct described in this Agreement and the Stipulated Statement of Facts (Exhibit A) for the duration of the Term of this Agreement plus three (3) additional years following the expiration or termination of this Agreement. The Company shall implement and maintain a litigation hold covering all such materials, and shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that relevant documents and records are not destroyed, altered, or rendered inaccessible. The Company shall notify the Government within forty-eight (48) hours of any inadvertent or unauthorized destruction of documents or records that may be subject to this preservation obligation.
124	
125	**[SECTION 7 --- CORPORATE COMPLIANCE PROGRAM ENHANCEMENTS]{.underline}**
126	
127	**[7.1 General Obligations]{.underline}**
128	
129	Greenvale shall implement and maintain an effective compliance and ethics program designed to prevent and detect violations of the Anti-Kickback Statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b, the False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 *et seq.*, and all other applicable federal and state laws, regulations, and company policies, throughout the Term of this Agreement. The compliance and ethics program shall be consistent with the principles set forth in Chapter 8 of the United States Sentencing Guidelines (Effective Compliance and Ethics Program) and with guidance issued by the Department of Justice, Criminal Division, regarding the Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs, as updated from time to time. The Company shall dedicate sufficient resources, including qualified personnel, to ensure the program\'s effectiveness.
130	
131	**[7.2 Chief Compliance Officer Reporting Line]{.underline}**
132	
133	Within sixty (60) days of the Execution Date, Greenvale shall restructure the reporting line of the Chief Compliance Officer (\"CCO\") so that the CCO reports directly to the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors, with a dotted-line reporting relationship to the Chief Executive Officer. The CCO shall have the authority and independence to report any compliance concerns directly to the Audit Committee without prior review or approval by the General Counsel or any other officer of the Company. The Audit Committee shall have sole authority over the hiring, compensation, evaluation, and termination of the CCO. The Company shall provide written confirmation of the restructured reporting line to the Government and the Independent Compliance Monitor within five (5) business days of its implementation.
134	
135	**[7.3 Speaker Program Reforms]{.underline}**
136	
137	Within ninety (90) days of the Execution Date, Greenvale shall implement the following reforms to its speaker programs for all branded pharmaceutical products:
138	
139	> \(a\) **Speaker Vetting Process.** The Company shall implement a new speaker vetting process requiring independent review by the compliance department of each proposed speaker\'s qualifications, speaking history, prescribing patterns, and prior payment history with the Company, before such speaker may be engaged for any event. The compliance department shall have authority to reject any proposed speaker engagement.
140	>
141	> \(b\) **Venue and Cost Restrictions.** Speaker events shall not be held at restaurants or other venues where the per-attendee cost of food, beverages, and venue rental exceeds one hundred fifty dollars (\$150). Speaker events shall be held in settings conducive to the exchange of medical or scientific information.
142	>
143	> \(c\) **Compliance Monitoring of Events.** All speaker events shall be attended by a compliance representative or, where in-person attendance is not feasible, monitored via live audiovisual recording. The compliance representative or recorded monitoring shall confirm that the speaker delivered the approved presentation in a meaningful manner and that attendees included healthcare professionals with a legitimate interest in the subject matter.
144	>
145	> \(d\) **Annual Honoraria Cap.** Annual speaker honoraria paid to any individual healthcare provider shall not exceed fifteen thousand dollars (\$15,000) in the aggregate, across all Greenvale speaker programs and branded products.
146	>
147	> \(e\) **High-Prescriber Prohibition.** The Company shall not engage any healthcare provider as a speaker if that provider has been identified as a high-prescriber of Neurovan or Cardivex within the preceding twelve (12) months. For purposes of this provision, a \"high-prescriber\" is defined as a healthcare provider whose prescribing volume for the relevant product falls within the top decile of providers in that provider\'s medical specialty, as measured by available claims data or prescription tracking data.
148	
149	**[7.4 Healthcare Provider Payment Tracking]{.underline}**
150	
151	Within one hundred twenty (120) days of the Execution Date, Greenvale shall implement an enhanced healthcare provider (\"HCP\") payment tracking system that records and cross-references all payments, transfers of value, and other remuneration to healthcare providers, including but not limited to speaker honoraria, consulting fees, advisory board fees, research grants, educational grants, charitable contributions, and any other transfer of value. The system shall generate automated alerts when any individual healthcare provider receives aggregate payments exceeding twenty-five thousand dollars (\$25,000) in any rolling twelve-month period. All such alerts shall be reviewed by the compliance department within ten (10) business days of generation, and a written determination shall be made regarding whether the aggregate payments are consistent with Company policy and applicable law.
152	
153	**[7.5 Annual Compliance Risk Assessment]{.underline}**
154	
155	Greenvale shall conduct an annual compliance risk assessment, led by the CCO and reviewed by the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors, covering all business units engaged in the marketing, sale, promotion, or distribution of pharmaceutical products. The annual risk assessment shall identify and evaluate key compliance risks, including but not limited to risks arising from speaker programs, consulting arrangements, healthcare provider interactions, government pricing and reporting, and interactions with government officials. The results of each annual risk assessment shall be documented in writing and provided to the Government and the Independent Compliance Monitor within thirty (30) days of completion.
156	
157	**[7.6 Compliance Training]{.underline}**
158	
159	Greenvale shall provide mandatory compliance training to all commercial personnel --- including, without limitation, all employees in the sales, marketing, medical affairs, and managed markets functions, as well as their respective managers and supervisors --- no less frequently than every ninety (90) days throughout the Term of this Agreement. Such training shall cover, at a minimum, the following subject areas:
160	
161	> \(a\) The Anti-Kickback Statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b, and the regulatory safe harbors established thereunder;
162	>
163	> \(b\) The False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 *et seq.*, and the legal standards for civil and criminal liability under the statute;
164	>
165	> \(c\) Greenvale\'s revised speaker program policies and procedures, including the reforms mandated by Section 7.3 of this Agreement;
166	>
167	> \(d\) Greenvale\'s policies and procedures governing healthcare provider engagements, including consulting arrangements, advisory boards, and other HCP interactions;
168	>
169	> \(e\) Reporting obligations under this Agreement, including the self-reporting obligations set forth in Section 6.4;
170	>
171	> \(f\) Consequences of non-compliance with applicable laws, regulations, company policies, and the terms of this Agreement, including potential criminal and civil penalties for individuals and the Company.
172	
173	Records of training completion, including the identity of each individual trained, the date and subject matter of each training session, and any assessments or certifications completed, shall be maintained by the Company and made available to the Independent Compliance Monitor and the Government upon request.
174	
175	**[7.7 Hotline and Reporting Mechanisms]{.underline}**
176	
177	Greenvale shall maintain a confidential reporting hotline and other mechanisms, including web-based reporting portals, through which employees and other stakeholders may report suspected compliance violations. Where permitted by applicable law, such reporting mechanisms shall allow anonymous reporting. The Company shall implement and enforce anti-retaliation policies to ensure that no employee who reports a suspected compliance violation in good faith is subjected to retaliation, adverse employment action, or other retribution. All reports received through the hotline or other mechanisms shall be reviewed and investigated by the compliance department, and the results of such investigations shall be documented and maintained for the duration of the Term plus three (3) years.
178	
179	**[7.8 Compliance Budget]{.underline}**
180	
181	Greenvale shall maintain a compliance program budget at a level sufficient to support the obligations set forth in this Agreement, and in no event less than six million dollars (\$6,000,000) per fiscal year during the Term. The compliance budget shall be approved by the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors and shall be separate from the Company\'s legal department budget. Any proposed reduction in the compliance budget below \$6,000,000 shall require the prior written approval of the Government and the Independent Compliance Monitor.
182	
183	**[7.9 Additional Compliance Reforms]{.underline}**
184	
185	In addition to the specific reforms set forth in Sections 7.2 through 7.8 above, Greenvale shall implement the following additional compliance program enhancements within one hundred twenty (120) days of the Execution Date, unless otherwise specified:
186	
187	> \(a\) **Anti-Retaliation Protections.** The Company shall adopt and publicize enhanced anti-retaliation policies that provide specific protections for employees who report suspected compliance violations, including protections against termination, demotion, reassignment, and other adverse employment actions. The Company shall designate a senior compliance official to serve as the anti-retaliation ombudsperson.
188	>
189	> \(b\) **Third-Party Due Diligence.** The Company shall implement enhanced due diligence procedures for all third-party intermediaries, including contract sales organizations, marketing agencies, medical education companies, and consultants, to assess compliance risks associated with such relationships before engagement and on an ongoing basis.
190	>
191	> \(c\) **Incentive Compensation Reforms.** The Company shall revise its incentive compensation structures for all commercial personnel to incorporate compliance metrics as a meaningful component of performance evaluation. No less than fifteen percent (15%) of variable compensation for sales and marketing personnel shall be tied to compliance objectives, including adherence to speaker program policies, timely completion of compliance training, and the absence of substantiated compliance violations.
192	>
193	> \(d\) **Senior Management Compliance Certifications.** On an annual basis, each member of the Company\'s executive leadership team, including the Chief Executive Officer, the Chief Financial Officer, the General Counsel, the Chief Compliance Officer, and each Senior Vice President and above, shall execute a written certification attesting that, to their knowledge, the Company\'s operations within their area of responsibility are in compliance with applicable laws, regulations, and the terms of this Agreement.
194	>
195	> \(e\) **Government Pricing and Reporting Compliance.** The Company shall conduct a review of its government pricing calculations and reporting practices, including Average Manufacturer Price, Best Price, and Federal Supply Schedule pricing, to ensure accuracy and compliance with applicable regulations.
196	>
197	> \(f\) **Board Oversight.** The Audit Committee of the Board of Directors shall receive quarterly reports from the CCO regarding the status of the Company\'s compliance program, any significant compliance incidents, and the progress of remedial actions undertaken pursuant to this Agreement.
198	
199	**[SECTION 8 --- MONETARY PENALTIES AND CIVIL SETTLEMENT]{.underline}**
200	
201	**[8.1 Criminal Monetary Penalty]{.underline}**
202	
203	Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. shall pay a criminal monetary penalty in the total amount of One Hundred Eighty-Seven Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$187,500,000), which has been calculated as follows:
204	
205	> \(a\) **Base Penalty.** The total alleged improper payments during the Relevant Period amount to \$20,500,000, consisting of \$14,300,000 in improper speaker honoraria (as described in Section 4.1 of this Agreement) and \$6,200,000 in improper consulting fees (as described in Section 4.2 of this Agreement). The base penalty is calculated by multiplying the total alleged improper payments by a factor of three (3), yielding a base penalty of \$61,500,000 (\$20,500,000 × 3 = \$61,500,000). This treble-damages multiplier reflects the seriousness of the conduct, the duration of the violation period, and the number of healthcare providers involved.
206	>
207	> \(b\) **Corporate Recidivism Multiplier.** In light of the Company\'s prior Corporate Integrity Agreement with the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services, entered into in 2014 in connection with the resolution of allegations of off-label promotion of Osteorin, which Corporate Integrity Agreement expired in 2019, the base penalty of \$61,500,000 is multiplied by a factor of two (2), yielding an adjusted base penalty of \$123,000,000 (\$61,500,000 × 2 = \$123,000,000). This recidivism multiplier reflects the Company\'s failure to maintain effective compliance controls following the conclusion of the prior enforcement action.
208	>
209	> \(c\) **Volume of Commerce Penalty.** An additional penalty of \$64,500,000, representing fifteen percent (15%) of relevant commerce during the Relevant Period, is added to the adjusted base penalty. This volume of commerce penalty reflects the scope and scale of the Company\'s commercial operations during the period of the violations and the Government\'s assessment of the profits derived from the unlawful conduct.
210	>
211	> \(d\) **Total Criminal Monetary Penalty.** The total criminal monetary penalty is the sum of the adjusted base penalty and the volume of commerce penalty: \$123,000,000 + \$64,500,000 = **\$187,500,000**.
212	
213	The Company acknowledges and agrees that this criminal monetary penalty is appropriate and proportionate given the nature, scope, and duration of the violations, the Company\'s prior enforcement history, and the need for deterrence.
214	
215	**[8.2 Civil Settlement]{.underline}**
216	
217	In addition to the criminal monetary penalty set forth in Section 8.1, Greenvale shall pay Fifty-Two Million Dollars (\$52,000,000) to resolve the Company\'s civil liability under the False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 *et seq.*, arising from the conduct described in this Agreement and the Stipulated Statement of Facts. This civil settlement payment is made as restitution to the United States of America for losses sustained by federal healthcare programs as a result of the submission of false or fraudulent claims caused by the Company\'s violations of the Anti-Kickback Statute. The civil settlement amount shall be paid to the United States Department of Justice in accordance with wire transfer instructions to be provided by the Government.
218	
219	**[8.3 Relator\'s Share]{.underline}**
220	
221	From the civil settlement amount of \$52,000,000, the United States shall pay Dr. Anita Patel, the *qui tam* relator, a relator\'s share of Twenty-Five Percent (25%) of the civil settlement proceeds, equal to Thirteen Million Dollars (\$13,000,000) (\$52,000,000 × 0.25 = \$13,000,000), pursuant to 31 U.S.C. § 3730(d). The relator\'s share reflects the Government\'s determination that Dr. Patel\'s *qui tam* complaint and subsequent cooperation substantially contributed to the investigation and resolution of this matter, consistent with the Government\'s intervention in the civil action.
222	
223	**[8.4 Payment Schedule]{.underline}**
224	
225	The criminal monetary penalty of \$187,500,000 shall be paid by Greenvale in four (4) installments as follows:
226	
227	> \(a\) **First Installment:** Fifty Million Dollars (\$50,000,000), due and payable upon execution of this Agreement;
228	>
229	> \(b\) **Second Installment:** Fifty Million Dollars (\$50,000,000), due and payable twelve (12) months after the Execution Date;
230	>
231	> \(c\) **Third Installment:** Fifty Million Dollars (\$50,000,000), due and payable twenty-four (24) months after the Execution Date;
232	>
233	> \(d\) **Fourth Installment:** Thirty-Seven Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$37,500,000), due and payable thirty-six (36) months after the Execution Date.
234	>
235	> **Total:** \$50,000,000 + \$50,000,000 + \$50,000,000 + \$37,500,000 = \$187,500,000.
236	
237	The civil settlement of Fifty-Two Million Dollars (\$52,000,000) shall be paid in a single lump sum upon execution of this Agreement.
238	
239	Accordingly, the total amount due and payable upon execution of this Agreement is One Hundred Two Million Dollars (\$102,000,000), consisting of the first installment of the criminal monetary penalty (\$50,000,000) and the civil settlement (\$52,000,000).
240	
241	All payments shall be made by electronic funds transfer to the account or accounts designated by the Government, in accordance with written wire transfer instructions to be provided by the United States Attorney\'s Office for the District of New Jersey no later than five (5) business days prior to each scheduled payment date.
242	
243	**[8.5 Late Payment Provisions]{.underline}**
244	
245	In the event that Greenvale fails to make any payment required under this Section 8 on or before the applicable due date, interest shall accrue on the unpaid amount from the due date until the date of payment at the rate specified by 28 U.S.C. § 1961, as calculated on the date of the first missed payment. 229	**STIPULATED STATEMENT OF FACTS**
230	
231	**[Introduction]{.underline}**
232	
233	The following facts are stipulated and agreed to by Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (\"the Company\") and the United States of America (the \"Government\"). These facts are true and correct. If this matter were to proceed to trial, the United States could prove these facts beyond a reasonable doubt through the testimony of witnesses and the introduction of documentary evidence.
234	
235	**[Part I --- Background]{.underline}**
236	
237	1\. Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware, publicly traded on the NASDAQ Stock Market under the ticker symbol \"GVPH,\" with its principal place of business at 400 Commerce Boulevard, Suite 1200, Princeton, New Jersey 08540.
238	
239	2\. During the Relevant Period (January 1, 2019 through December 31, 2022), Greenvale manufactured, marketed, and sold three branded pharmaceutical products in the United States: Neurovan, indicated for the treatment of epilepsy; Cardivex, indicated for the treatment of atrial fibrillation; and Osteorin, indicated for the treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. All three products were prescribed by healthcare providers and dispensed to patients, including patients enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and other federal healthcare programs.
240	
241	3\. During the Relevant Period, the following individuals held the positions indicated: Dr. Marcus Ellison served as Chief Executive Officer; Janet Huang served as General Counsel; Thomas Bridwell served as Chief Financial Officer; and Patricia Knowles served as Chief Compliance Officer. Kevin Driscoll served as Regional Sales Director for the Northeast Region, Maria Santos served as Regional Sales Director for the Southeast Region, and Dr. Leonard Kwan served as Vice President of Medical Affairs until his departure from the Company in March 2022.
242	
243	4\. Greenvale\'s commercial organization consisted of approximately 1,200 sales representatives and 85 district managers organized across six geographic regions. The Company\'s sales and marketing divisions reported to the Chief Commercial Officer, who in turn reported to the Chief Executive Officer.
244	
245	**[Part II --- The Speaker Programs]{.underline}**
246	
247	5\. During the Relevant Period, Greenvale operated nationwide speaker programs for Neurovan and Cardivex. The stated purpose of these speaker programs was to provide medical education to healthcare providers about the clinical uses, safety profiles, and efficacy data for Neurovan and Cardivex. Under these programs, Greenvale engaged healthcare providers as paid speakers to deliver presentations to other healthcare providers at events organized by the Company\'s sales representatives and district managers.
248	
249	6\. Over the four-year Relevant Period, Greenvale conducted approximately 4,200 speaker events per year, for a total of approximately 16,800 speaker events. Total speaker honoraria paid by the Company during the Relevant Period amounted to approximately \$38,600,000, allocated as follows: approximately \$8,400,000 in fiscal year 2019; approximately \$10,200,000 in fiscal year 2020; approximately \$11,100,000 in fiscal year 2021; and approximately \$8,900,000 in fiscal year 2022.
250	
251	7\. Regional Sales Directors Kevin Driscoll and Maria Santos actively encouraged sales representatives and district managers within their respective regions to recruit high-prescribing healthcare providers as speakers. Driscoll and Santos directed their subordinates to prioritize physicians with the highest prescribing volume for Neurovan and Cardivex when selecting speakers for program events, regardless of whether those physicians possessed particular expertise or qualifications as medical educators. Internal communications between Driscoll, Santos, and their subordinates demonstrate that the primary purpose of many speaker engagements was to reward high-prescribing physicians with honoraria rather than to deliver legitimate medical education.
252	
253	8\. Approximately 1,150 of the 16,800 speaker events conducted during the Relevant Period were sham programs that served no legitimate educational purpose. At these sham events, one or more of the following conditions was present: (a) the engaged speaker did not deliver a genuine medical education presentation, or delivered a significantly abbreviated or perfunctory version of the approved slide deck; (b) the audience consisted primarily or exclusively of the speaker\'s own office staff, including medical assistants, receptionists, and billing personnel who had no prescribing authority and no clinical need for the information; or (c) the event was held at a high-end restaurant where the primary activity was dining and socializing, with little or no meaningful educational content delivered.
254	
255	9\. At minimum, \$14,300,000 in speaker honoraria paid during the Relevant Period was in connection with sham speaker events that served no legitimate educational purpose. These payments constituted remuneration to healthcare providers intended to induce and reward prescriptions for Neurovan and Cardivex, including prescriptions for patients enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and other federal healthcare programs.
256	
257	10\. The speaker program structure was approved by Dr. Leonard Kwan in his capacity as Vice President of Medical Affairs. Dr. Kwan authorized the continued expansion of speaker programs in 2020 and 2021 despite receiving internal reports indicating concerns about the educational value and compliance of certain events.
258	
259	**[Part III --- The Consulting Arrangements]{.underline}**
260	
261	11\. During the Relevant Period, Greenvale maintained consulting arrangements with approximately 47 high-prescribing healthcare providers. These consulting arrangements took various forms, including advisory board participation, market research engagements, and clinical input agreements. Under these arrangements, the engaged healthcare providers were paid consulting fees for participation in advisory board meetings, completion of market research surveys, and provision of clinical input on the Company\'s marketing and promotional strategies for Neurovan and Cardivex.
262	
263	12\. Total consulting fees paid to these 47 healthcare providers during the Relevant Period amounted to approximately \$6,200,000, allocated as follows: approximately \$1,100,000 in fiscal year 2019; approximately \$1,600,000 in fiscal year 2020; approximately \$1,900,000 in fiscal year 2021; and approximately \$1,600,000 in fiscal year 2022. Individual consulting fees ranged from approximately \$40,000 to approximately \$225,000 per year per healthcare provider.
264	
265	13\. The consulting fees paid to these healthcare providers were disproportionate to the services actually rendered. Many of the advisory board meetings were brief, poorly documented, and did not result in meaningful clinical input that was utilized by the Company. Several healthcare providers received consulting fees for market research surveys that consisted of a small number of questions and required minimal time to complete. The fees paid for these engagements substantially exceeded the fair market value of the services rendered.
266	
267	14\. Dr. Leonard Kwan approved the consulting fee arrangements in his capacity as Vice President of Medical Affairs. Dr. Kwan selected the healthcare providers to be engaged as consultants based, in significant part, on their prescribing volume for Neurovan and Cardivex. The consulting arrangements were designed to maintain and strengthen relationships with high-prescribing physicians and to incentivize continued and increased prescribing of Neurovan and Cardivex.
268	
269	15\. The consulting fees constituted remuneration to healthcare providers intended to induce and reward prescriptions for Neurovan and Cardivex, in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute.
270	
271	**[Part IV --- Knowledge and Intent]{.underline}**
272	
273	16\. Senior management, including members of the executive team, were aware of and tacitly approved the use of speaker programs as a vehicle for rewarding high-prescribing physicians. The executive team received periodic reports that included data on speaker program expenditures, the number of speaker events conducted, and the prescribing patterns of engaged speakers. Despite the availability of this information, senior management did not take adequate steps to ensure that speaker programs were operated in compliance with the Anti-Kickback Statute or the Company\'s own policies.
274	
275	17\. The Company\'s compliance department identified hundreds of potentially problematic speaker events during the Relevant Period. Between 2019 and 2022, the compliance department flagged 312 speaker events as potentially non-compliant based on internal monitoring criteria, including events with unusually small audience sizes, events where the audience consisted predominantly of the speaker\'s own staff, and events with excessive food and beverage expenditures. Of these 312 flagged events, only 41 were actually cancelled. The remaining 271 events proceeded after cursory review by district managers, who were themselves incentivized by the volume of speaker programs in their territories. This pattern reflected a corporate culture that prioritized revenue generation over legal compliance.
276	
277	18\. Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. knowingly and willfully violated the Anti-Kickback Statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b, by implementing and maintaining speaker programs and consulting arrangements that were designed to, and did, induce healthcare providers to prescribe Neurovan and Cardivex. The Company\'s speaker programs and consulting arrangements constituted a scheme to pay remuneration to healthcare providers in exchange for prescribing the Company\'s products, including products dispensed to patients enrolled in federal healthcare programs. The remuneration took the form of speaker honoraria and consulting fees that were not paid for legitimate services but rather as rewards for past prescribing and inducements for future prescribing.
278	
279	19\. The Company\'s failure to take meaningful corrective action in response to the compliance department\'s repeated identification of problematic speaker events, and the Company\'s continued expansion of speaker program activity despite knowledge of compliance risks, demonstrate that the violations were not the result of isolated misconduct by individual employees but rather reflected systemic failures of corporate oversight and a deliberate prioritization of commercial objectives over compliance with federal healthcare laws.
280	
281	**[Part V --- Compliance Program Deficiencies]{.underline}**
282	
283	20\. During the Relevant Period, Greenvale\'s compliance program suffered from significant structural and operational deficiencies that contributed to the violations described herein. The Company\'s Chief Compliance Officer, Patricia Knowles, reported to the General Counsel, Janet Huang, rather than reporting directly to the Board of Directors\' Audit Committee. This reporting structure compromised the independence of the compliance function and created a potential conflict of interest, as the General Counsel was responsible for both the Company\'s legal strategy and its compliance oversight.
284	
285	21\. The compliance department\'s annual operating budget was reduced by approximately 18%, from \$4,800,000 in fiscal year 2019 to \$3,936,000 in fiscal year 2020. This budget reduction occurred during a period when speaker program activity was expanding in both scope and expenditure, thereby further constraining the compliance department\'s ability to effectively monitor commercial activities.
286	
287	22\. As noted in Paragraph 17, the compliance department flagged 312 speaker events as potentially problematic between 2019 and 2022, but only 41 of those events were actually cancelled. The remaining 271 events proceeded, in most cases after review by district-level commercial management rather than by independent compliance personnel. This pattern demonstrated that the compliance function lacked the authority, resources, and independence necessary to effectively prevent and detect violations.
288	
289	23\. Greenvale previously entered into a Corporate Integrity Agreement with the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services in 2014, in connection with the resolution of allegations of off-label promotion of Osteorin. That Corporate Integrity Agreement had a five-year term and expired in 2019. The Company\'s failure to maintain effective compliance controls following the expiration of the CIA, and the recurrence of compliance failures involving a different form of unlawful conduct (kickbacks rather than off-label promotion), demonstrates a persistent pattern of inadequate corporate compliance.
290	
291	**[Part VI --- Impact on Federal Healthcare Programs]{.underline}**
292	
293	24\. As a direct result of the improper inducements described in this Stipulated Statement of Facts, healthcare providers who received speaker honoraria and consulting fees from Greenvale prescribed Neurovan and Cardivex to patients enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, the Veterans Health Administration, and other federal healthcare programs. Claims for reimbursement for these prescriptions were submitted to, and paid by, federal healthcare programs.
294	
295	25\. Claims for payment that were caused by violations of the Anti-Kickback Statute are false or fraudulent claims within the meaning of the False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 *et seq.* The improper inducements paid by Greenvale caused the submission of thousands of false or fraudulent claims for reimbursement to federal healthcare programs during the Relevant Period.
296	
297	26\. Total combined revenue for Neurovan and Cardivex during the Relevant Period (fiscal years 2019 through 2022) was approximately \$4.12 billion. While the Government does not allege that all prescriptions for Neurovan and Cardivex during the Relevant Period were procured through kickbacks, the Company\'s widespread use of improper speaker programs and consulting arrangements tainted a substantial portion of the commercial activity associated with these products.
298	
299	27\. The United States and its federal healthcare programs were harmed by the submission of false or fraudulent claims resulting from the Company\'s violations of the Anti-Kickback Statute.

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL =E2=80=94 ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNE=
Y WORK PRODUCT

From: Sarah Lin <slin@meridiancapitaladvisors.com>
To: Janet Huang <jhuang@greenvalepharma.com>
Cc: Thomas Bridwell <tbridwell@greenvalepharma.com>
Date: December 16, 2024, 3:47 PM EST
Subject: BioNovus Acquisition =E2=80=94 DPA Implications and Timeline Conside=
rations

Janet,

Thank you for making time earlier today for the call with Thomas and me regar=
ding the BioNovus acquisition timeline. I've now had a chance to review the s=
ummary of draft DPA terms you shared with us under the common interest agreem=
ent, and I want to flag several concerns from a deal-execution and financing =
standpoint that I believe require immediate attention.

As you know, Meridian is advising Greenvale on the pending acquisition of Bio=
Novus Therapeutics, Inc. for $340 million (all cash), with an expected LOI si=
gning of March 15, 2025 and an anticipated closing in Q3 2025. After reviewin=
g the draft DPA terms in the context of that timeline, I see two significant =
risk areas that could jeopardize the transaction.

**1. Successor Liability Clause**

The draft DPA's successor liability provision is, in my view, the single most=
 consequential clause for the BioNovus acquisition. As I read the summary, th=
e DPA binds "all successors, assigns, and any entity that acquires all or sub=
stantially all of the assets or equity of the Company." I see three specific =
problems with this language:

First, **there is no materiality threshold**. The clause does not define "sub=
stantially all." Does Greenvale's acquisition of BioNovus =E2=80=94 a $340 mi=
llion transaction by a company with a $6.1 billion market cap =E2=80=94 const=
itute acquiring "substantially all" of anything? More to the point, the claus=
e is ambiguous as to directionality. It could be read to apply not only to an=
 entity that acquires Greenvale, but also to entities that Greenvale acquires=
 =E2=80=94 i.e., BioNovus becoming a Greenvale subsidiary. The language simpl=
y does not distinguish between these scenarios.

Second, **there is no government consent requirement**. The clause automatica=
lly binds successors without any process for the government to consent to or =
even acknowledge the transfer of obligations. This means that BioNovus, once =
acquired and made a subsidiary of Greenvale, could be argued to fall under th=
e DPA's compliance mandates and monitor oversight by operation of the clause =
itself =E2=80=94 without the USAO ever having considered or approved that res=
ult.

Third, and perhaps most immediately concerning from a deal perspective, are t=
he **monitor implications**. If the monitor =E2=80=94 Thornfield Consulting G=
roup =E2=80=94 has access to "all company records, personnel, and board meeti=
ngs" without limitation, as I understand from the summary, then that access w=
ould arguably extend post-closing to BioNovus's operations, R&D data (includi=
ng all clinical data for BNV-401, their lead compound for treatment-resistant=
 depression), and personnel. I cannot overstate how significant a concern thi=
s will be for BioNovus's management team and board. It has the potential to b=
e a deal-breaker.

Has the Whitfield & Crane team assessed whether the successor clause would ap=
ply to acquired subsidiaries? Can we negotiate a carve-out, or at a minimum, =
a requirement for government consent before DPA obligations extend to newly a=
cquired entities?

**2. Financing and Credit Facility Concerns**

Turning to the financial side, which I know Thomas has been focused on: the c=
ombined DPA payments total $239.5 million ($187.5M criminal penalty plus $52.=
0M civil settlement). The signing-date cash outlay alone is $102.0 million =
=E2=80=94 the $50.0M first criminal installment plus the $52.0M civil settlem=
ent paid as a lump sum at execution.

Based on Greenvale's September 30, 2024 10-Q, the company has approximately $=
420 million in cash and equivalents. The BioNovus acquisition at $340 million=
 (all cash) plus the DPA signing-date payment of $102.0 million totals $442 m=
illion =E2=80=94 exceeding available cash by $22 million. And that is before =
accounting for the ongoing DPA installments ($50.0M at 12 months, $50.0M at 2=
4 months, and $37.5M at 36 months) and the estimated monitor costs (approxima=
tely $4.5M per year, or $13.5M over the three-year term).

Greenvale will almost certainly need to draw additional funds on the $500 mil=
lion revolving credit facility, of which $320 million is currently drawn, lea=
ving $180 million available. But this brings me to the critical concern.

**The revolving credit facility with Trident National Bank contains a materia=
l legal proceeding cross-default provision that is triggered by any settlemen=
t or judgment exceeding $75 million.** The DPA's combined $239.5 million in p=
ayments vastly exceeds this threshold. Janet, I need to ask directly: **has G=
reenvale obtained, or begun the process of obtaining, a waiver from Trident N=
ational Bank?**

If execution of the DPA triggers a cross-default under the revolver, Trident =
National Bank would have the right to accelerate the $320 million drawn balan=
ce. I would also flag the potential for cross-acceleration to the $650 millio=
n in 4.25% senior notes due 2029. In a worst-case scenario, the entire $970 m=
illion debt stack could be put at risk.

Without a lender waiver in hand before the anticipated February 1, 2025 DPA e=
xecution date, the financing for both the DPA payments and the BioNovus acqui=
sition is uncertain. I have to be candid: Meridian cannot advise the board to=
 proceed with the LOI signing on March 15, 2025 until this is resolved.

**3. Timeline Pressure**

The proximity of key dates creates significant execution risk:

- DPA negotiation session: January 15, 2025
- Anticipated DPA execution: February 1, 2025
- BioNovus LOI signing: March 15, 2025
- BioNovus closing: Q3 2025

If the successor liability clause is not resolved before the DPA is signed on=
 February 1, it becomes a fixed feature of the deal landscape, and we will ha=
ve to structure the BioNovus acquisition around it =E2=80=94 or walk away fro=
m the transaction. I strongly urge that the successor clause and monitor scop=
e be treated as top-priority items in the January 15 negotiation session.

Can we schedule a call with you, Elena Vasquez, and your team before the holi=
days to align on these points? My team is available through December 23. I'd =
like to make sure we are in lockstep before the year-end break.

Best regards,

Sarah Lin
Managing Director
Meridian Capital Advisors
T: (212) 555-0184
slin@meridiancapitaladvisors.com

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL =E2=80=94 ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNE=
Y WORK PRODUCT

From: Janet Huang <jhuang@greenvalepharma.com>
To: Sarah Lin <slin@meridiancapitaladvisors.com>
Cc: Thomas Bridwell <tbridwell@greenvalepharma.com>
Date: December 18, 2024, 10:22 AM EST
Subject: RE: BioNovus Acquisition =E2=80=94 DPA Implications and Timeline Con=
siderations

Sarah,

Thank you for the thorough analysis. Your concerns are well-taken, and I appr=
eciate the specificity =E2=80=94 it's exactly the kind of diligence we need r=
ight now. I've shared your email with Elena Vasquez and the Whitfield & Crane=
 team under the common interest agreement.

Let me address your two principal concerns in turn.

**Successor Liability Clause**

I share your concern. The clause is, frankly, poorly drafted from Greenvale's=
 perspective. It was clearly written to contemplate a scenario in which Green=
vale itself is acquired =E2=80=94 a change-of-control protection for the gove=
rnment's enforcement interest. It does not appear to account for the far more=
 likely scenario in which Greenvale is the acquirer.

That said, I want to be transparent that Whitfield & Crane is currently condu=
cting a comprehensive review of the full draft DPA =E2=80=94 Elena's senior a=
ssociate is beginning that review this week, on December 20 =E2=80=94 and the=
 successor clause is on their list of priority issues. My preliminary read al=
igns with yours: the clause's reference to "any entity that acquires all or s=
ubstantially all of the assets or equity of the Company" is directed at a cha=
nge-of-control scenario for Greenvale, but the broader "successors and assign=
s" language is open-ended enough to sweep in acquired subsidiaries, particula=
rly if BioNovus becomes a wholly owned subsidiary that is integrated into Gre=
envale's commercial operations (which is, of course, the plan).

I will raise this with Elena as a priority negotiation item for the January 1=
5 session. Our proposed approach would be to seek either: (a) explicit langua=
ge clarifying that the DPA applies only to Greenvale and its existing operati=
ons as of the execution date, with newly acquired entities excluded unless sp=
ecifically approved by the USAO; or (b) at minimum, a requirement that the go=
vernment consent before DPA obligations extend to any post-execution acquisit=
ion target. I would welcome your input on which formulation Meridian views as=
 more protective from a deal-execution standpoint.

I should also note that Dr. Ellison is aware of the tension between the DPA t=
imeline and the BioNovus timeline and has asked that the team keep the board =
informed of developments on both fronts.

**Credit Facility / Lender Waiver**

I have to acknowledge that this is a critical gap. To answer your question di=
rectly: **Greenvale has not yet requested a waiver from Trident National Bank=
.** The reasoning has been that we wanted greater clarity on the final DPA te=
rms before approaching the lender, as the waiver request will need to describ=
e the settlement amount and terms with specificity, and we did not want to en=
gage Trident prematurely with numbers that might shift during negotiation.

However, I fully acknowledge your point that the timeline is tight. The DPA i=
s anticipated to be executed on February 1, 2025. The credit facility waiver =
process requires consent of lenders holding at least 66.7% of outstanding com=
mitments and a minimum 15-business-day notice period. Working backward, that =
means a formal waiver request would need to be submitted no later than mid-Ja=
nuary to have a waiver in hand by February 1.

I will discuss with Thomas this week about initiating the waiver process now,=
 even with the DPA terms still in negotiation. We may need to provide Trident=
 National Bank with a range of potential settlement amounts rather than a fin=
al number =E2=80=94 not ideal, but better than running up against the clock.

Your liquidity analysis is also well-founded. I agree that the combined cash =
demands of the DPA signing-date payment ($102.0M) and the BioNovus acquisitio=
n ($340M) will require very careful cash management and almost certainly addi=
tional draws on the revolver =E2=80=94 which makes the waiver not just a tech=
nical requirement but an operational necessity.

One additional point I want to flag: the draft DPA itself contains no conditi=
on or provision allowing Greenvale to delay execution pending receipt of thir=
d-party consents such as a lender waiver. If we cannot obtain the waiver by F=
ebruary 1, we may face the choice of executing the DPA and risking a cross-de=
fault or requesting a delay from the USAO, which carries its own risks. I pla=
n to raise with Elena whether we should negotiate a condition into the DPA th=
at would allow execution to be deferred for a reasonable period pending recei=
pt of necessary third-party consents.

**Proposed Call**

I'd like to suggest we convene a call this Friday, December 20, with Elena Va=
squez, Thomas Bridwell, and your team at Meridian. Can you confirm availabili=
ty? I'll coordinate with Elena's office and circulate a dial-in.

Please continue to treat all of this as privileged and confidential.

Best,

Janet Huang
General Counsel
Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
T: (617) 555-0342
jhuang@greenvalepharma.com

 Considerations

Janet,

Thank you for the candid update. Friday works =E2=80=94 I'll have my team ava=
ilable.

Before the call, I want to add a few additional observations on deal risk tha=
t I think should frame the discussion.

From Meridian's perspective, the successor liability clause and the cross-def=
ault risk remain the two most significant DPA-related obstacles to the BioNov=
us acquisition. But I want to flag an additional wrinkle on the monitor side =
that I've been thinking through since Monday.

Even if the successor clause is successfully narrowed =E2=80=94 say, through =
the carve-out approach you described =E2=80=94 the monitor's broad access to =
"all company records" could still independently expose BioNovus's proprietary=
 R&D and clinical data to Thornfield Consulting Group. The BNV-401 program fo=
r treatment-resistant depression is the crown jewel of BioNovus's pipeline, a=
nd the clinical data underlying it is extraordinarily sensitive. Post-closing=
, if BioNovus is integrated into Greenvale's operations, there may be no clea=
n line between "Greenvale records" subject to the monitor and "BioNovus recor=
ds" that should be excluded.

I also want to raise a concern I have not seen addressed: **Thornfield Consul=
ting Group has prior advisory work with Vantage BioPharma**, which as you kno=
w is a direct competitor of Greenvale in several therapeutic areas. The prosp=
ect of competitively sensitive BioNovus R&D and clinical data flowing through=
 a monitor that has advised a competitor is a meaningful risk. BioNovus's boa=
rd and investors will ask about this. We need an answer.

I would ask whether the January 15 negotiation could include scope limitation=
s on the monitor =E2=80=94 specifically, restricting Thornfield's access to t=
he business units involved in the underlying conduct (the Neurovan and Cardiv=
ex commercial operations) rather than the entire Greenvale enterprise. This w=
ould protect BioNovus data post-closing and mitigate the Thornfield/Vantage c=
oncern.

One final point on the financial picture. The total financial commitment unde=
r the DPA =E2=80=94 $239.5M in settlement payments plus an estimated $13.5M i=
n monitor costs =E2=80=94 comes to approximately $253.0M over three years. Ad=
d the $340M BioNovus acquisition price and you're looking at total commitment=
s of roughly $593M over the next three years. Against current cash of $420M a=
nd $180M in available revolver capacity, total liquidity is approximately $60=
0M. That leaves effectively no margin for error, and none of these figures ac=
count for operating cash needs or the ongoing DPA installments reducing liqui=
dity in years two and three. This is a boardroom-level discussion, and I'd su=
ggest Thomas prepare a detailed pro forma liquidity analysis that maps out th=
e quarterly cash demands from both the DPA and the BioNovus acquisition again=
st projected operating cash flows and available credit.

I'll have my team dialed in on Friday. Can you circulate the call details whe=
n confirmed?

Best,

Sarah Lin
Managing Director
Meridian Capital Advisors
T: (212) 555-0184
slin@meridiancapitaladvisors.com

Sarah,

Friday call is confirmed for 10:00 AM EST. I've added Elena Vasquez to this c=
hain so that her team at Whitfield & Crane can participate directly. Dial-in =

A few updates based on conversations this afternoon:

**Trident National Bank / Lender Waiver.** I spoke with Thomas Bridwell after=
 our exchange. Thomas is initiating contact with the relationship team at Tri=
dent National Bank to begin the waiver discussion process on an informal basi=
s. The formal waiver request will follow once the DPA terms are further along=
, but we agree with your assessment that we cannot afford to wait. Thomas is =
also preparing the pro forma liquidity analysis you requested =E2=80=94 we ex=
pect to have a working draft available for the Friday call or early next week.

**Whitfield & Crane DPA Review.** I can confirm that Elena's team =E2=80=94 E=
lena and the senior associate handling the DPA review =E2=80=94 are catalogui=
ng all DPA provisions with M&A and financing implications, including the succ=
essor liability clause, the monitor's scope of access, and the absence of a t=
hird-party consent condition. Your point about Thornfield's prior advisory re=
lationship with Vantage BioPharma is noted and will be added to the analysis.=
 That is exactly the kind of issue we need to surface now, not after closing.

**January 15 Negotiation Strategy.** I have a preliminary discussion schedule=
d with Elena next week regarding our negotiation strategy for the January 15 =
session with AUSA Patricia Moreno and AUSA David Kesselman. I will ensure tha=
t the successor liability clause and monitor scope limitations are among the =
top-priority items we raise. Your suggestion to seek restrictions limiting mo=
nitor access to the Neurovan and Cardivex commercial operations =E2=80=94 the=
 business units involved in the underlying conduct =E2=80=94 is a strong one =
and will be central to our proposed approach.

**One request:** Could you have the Meridian team prepare a brief summary of =
how comparable DPAs in the pharmaceutical industry have handled successor obl=
igations in the context of pending or anticipated acquisitions? If there is p=
recedent for carve-outs or acquisition-specific exclusions, that would signif=
icantly strengthen our negotiation position with the USAO. Even two or three =
relevant examples would be valuable.

I want to reiterate the importance of keeping this entire discussion privileg=
ed and confidential. The DPA terms are not yet public, and our discussions re=
garding the interplay between the DPA and the BioNovus acquisition are covere=
d by the common interest agreement between Greenvale and Meridian Capital Adv=
isors. Please ensure distribution is limited accordingly.

We'll speak Friday. Thank you, Sarah =E2=80=94 your team's work on this has b=

181	**6.2 Material Legal Proceeding Default (Section 7.1(h)) --- CRITICAL PROVISION**
182	
183	The full operative language of Section 7.1(h) of the Credit Agreement provides as follows:
184	
185	> *\"An Event of Default shall exist if the Borrower or any Subsidiary shall (i) enter into any settlement or consent to any judgment, order, or decree, in connection with any litigation, investigation, governmental proceeding, or regulatory action, in an amount (whether payable as a fine, penalty, restitution, disgorgement, settlement payment, or otherwise) exceeding \$75,000,000 individually or in the aggregate during any twelve-month period, or (ii) become subject to any judgment, order, or decree for monetary damages or penalties exceeding \$75,000,000 individually or in the aggregate during any twelve-month period.\"*
186	
187	**Critical Analysis for DPA Review:**
188	
189	The DPA\'s combined criminal penalty (\$187,500,000) and civil settlement (\$52,000,000) total **\$239,500,000**, which exceeds the \$75,000,000 threshold by **\$164,500,000** --- more than three times the covenant threshold. The signing-date payment alone (\$102,000,000, comprising \$50,000,000 in criminal penalty first installment and \$52,000,000 in civil settlement lump sum) independently exceeds the threshold by \$27,000,000. Each subsequent installment of the criminal penalty --- \$50,000,000 at twelve months, \$50,000,000 at twenty-four months, and \$37,500,000 at thirty-six months --- also exceeds the threshold on an individual basis, though the provision triggers upon the Borrower\'s entry into a \"settlement or consent\" rather than upon each individual payment date. Accordingly, the entire \$239,500,000 amount would trigger the provision at the time of DPA execution, not incrementally on each installment date.
190	
191	The provision\'s broadly drafted parenthetical --- \"(whether payable as a fine, penalty, restitution, disgorgement, settlement payment, or otherwise)\" --- captures the full spectrum of monetary obligations that may arise under the DPA. The parenthetical does not distinguish between criminal penalties, civil settlements, and restitution; all forms of monetary obligation are encompassed. There is no carve-out or exception for government-mandated payments, regulatory settlements, or deferred prosecution agreements.
192	
193	A deferred prosecution agreement is, at minimum, a form of \"settlement\" with a governmental authority in connection with a \"governmental proceeding\" or \"investigation.\" Even if one were to argue that a DPA is technically not a \"settlement\" because the criminal information is filed and not dismissed until the deferral period expires, it is clearly a \"consent to\" a \"judgment, order, or decree\" in connection with a governmental proceeding. The provision appears to be clearly and unambiguously triggered by the execution of the DPA.
194	
195	**Consequence if Triggered:** If an Event of Default arises under Section 7.1(h), the remedies described in Section 6.4 below become available to the Required Lenders, including acceleration of all outstanding obligations and termination of the lending commitment. The implications for the Company are severe and are summarized in Section 11 below.

198	
199	Section 7.1(f) of the Credit Agreement provides:
200	
201	> *\"An Event of Default shall exist if the Borrower or any Subsidiary shall default under any Indebtedness in an aggregate principal amount exceeding \$25,000,000 if such default results in such Indebtedness becoming or being declared due and payable prior to its stated maturity.\"*
202	
203	The Company\'s **\$650,000,000** in 4.25% Senior Notes due 2029 (the \"Senior Notes\") were issued pursuant to an Indenture that contains its own cross-default provision. Specifically, the Senior Notes Indenture provides that a default under \"any credit facility or material debt instrument\" of the Company constitutes an event of default under the Indenture if such default results in, or permits the holder or trustee to declare, the acceleration of such credit facility or debt instrument. If the revolving credit facility enters an Event of Default due to Section 7.1(h), and the Required Lenders direct acceleration of the revolver, the Senior Notes Indenture would be triggered, resulting in potential cross-acceleration of the Senior Notes.

209	  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------

While the Company\'s total assets may be sufficient to cover these obligations, forced acceleration would be severely disruptive to the Company\'s operations, could trigger going-concern qualifications in the Company\'s audited financial statements, and would likely result in a material decline in the Company\'s stock price and credit ratings.

220	
221	Upon the occurrence and continuance of an Event of Default under Section 7.1(h) or any other subsection of Section 7.1:
222	
223	> \(a\) The **Required Lenders** (lenders holding more than 50% of total commitments) may direct the Administrative Agent to declare all outstanding Obligations immediately due and payable, without presentment, demand, protest, or further notice of any kind;
224	>
225	> \(b\) The **Commitment** of each Lender to make further advances under the revolving credit facility is **automatically terminated** upon the occurrence of an Event of Default (no lender direction required); and

This is a critical distinction: even if the Required Lenders do not elect to accelerate, the occurrence of an Event of Default would reduce Greenvale\'s available liquidity from \$180,000,000 (current undrawn revolver capacity) to \$0 in undrawn revolver capacity, leaving only the \$420,000,000 in cash on hand (which would itself be reduced by the DPA signing-date payments to approximately \$318,000,000). 307	**\"Required Lenders\"** means, at any time, Lenders having Commitments representing at least **66⅔%** of the aggregate outstanding Commitments, or, if the Commitments have been terminated, Lenders holding at least 66⅔% of the aggregate outstanding principal amount of the Loans.
308	
309	**\"Material Subsidiary\"** means any Subsidiary of the Borrower with (a) total assets exceeding 5% of the consolidated total assets of the Borrower and its Subsidiaries or (b) revenues exceeding 5% of the consolidated total revenues of the Borrower and its Subsidiaries, in each case as of the end of and for the most recently completed fiscal year.
310	
311	**[Section 11: Summary of Key Risk Points for DPA Review]{.underline}**
312	
313	Based on the foregoing analysis of the Credit Agreement, the following key risk points are identified for the DPA review team:
314	
315	**(1) Cross-Default Trigger Is Virtually Certain.** The \$239,500,000 in combined DPA payments (\$187,500,000 criminal penalty + \$52,000,000 civil settlement) exceeds the \$75,000,000 Material Legal Proceeding Threshold by more than \$164,500,000. The operative language of Section 7.1(h) is broad and unambiguous, capturing settlements with governmental authorities \"whether payable as a fine, penalty, restitution, disgorgement, settlement payment, or otherwise.\" Execution of the DPA will constitute an Event of Default under Section 7.1(h) unless a waiver is obtained from the Required Lenders in advance.
316	
317	**(2) Cross-Acceleration Risk to Senior Notes.** An Event of Default under the revolving credit facility could trigger a cross-default under the \$650,000,000 Senior Notes Indenture, exposing the Company to potential acceleration of **\$970,000,000** in total debt --- the Company\'s entire funded debt stack.
318	
319	**(3) Liquidity Freeze.** Even absent acceleration by the Required Lenders, the occurrence of an Event of Default automatically terminates the Borrower\'s ability to draw on the \$180,000,000 of undrawn revolver capacity. This elimination of available credit, combined with the DPA signing-date payment of \$102,000,000, would significantly constrain the Company\'s liquidity position.
320	
321	**(4) BioNovus Acquisition Blocked.** The \"no Event of Default\" condition in the Permitted Acquisition provisions (Sections 4.3(a) and 9.1(b)) would prevent the BioNovus acquisition (\$340,000,000 all-cash) from proceeding without first obtaining a waiver of the Event of Default. This creates a direct link between the DPA resolution and the Company\'s strategic growth plans.
322	
323	**(5) Waiver Timeline Is Critical.** The minimum 20-Business-Day waiver process (5 days for Administrative Agent circulation + 15 days for lender response) means Greenvale must submit a formal waiver request to Trident National Bank **no later than approximately January 3, 2025**, to have any realistic prospect of obtaining the waiver before the anticipated February 1, 2025 DPA execution date. As of the date of this summary, approximately 8 Business Days remain before this deadline.
324	
325	**(6) Silence Is Rejection.** Under the Credit Agreement\'s waiver mechanics, lender non-response is deemed a rejection. Affirmative written consent from lenders holding at least 66⅔% of aggregate Commitments is required. Passive or disengaged lenders cannot be counted toward the consent threshold.
326	
327	**(7) DPA Contains No Savings Clause.** The draft DPA as currently presented does not condition execution on the Company\'s obtaining necessary lender consents, waivers, or third-party approvals. The DPA does not include a condition precedent allowing reasonable time to secure such consents before the agreement becomes effective. This is a significant gap that should be addressed in the January 15, 2025 negotiation session with the USAO.
328	
329	**Recommendation:** The DPA review team should immediately take the following coordinated actions:
330	
331	> \(a\) Engage Thomas Bridwell (CFO) and Meridian Capital Advisors (Sarah Lin, engagement lead) to begin informal lender outreach to Trident National Bank and the key syndicate members to socialize the anticipated DPA resolution and gauge lender receptivity to a waiver;
332	>
333	> \(b\) Prepare and submit a formal waiver request package to Trident National Bank no later than January 3, 2025, including a summary of the DPA terms, a pro forma financial analysis demonstrating the Company\'s ability to service the DPA payments while maintaining covenant compliance, and a narrative addressing the long-term benefits to the Company of resolving the federal investigation; and
334	>
335	> \(c\) Concurrently, negotiate with the USAO at the January 15, 2025 session for the inclusion of a condition precedent in the DPA allowing a reasonable period (not less than 30 days) following execution for the Company to obtain necessary third-party consents, or alternatively, for a delayed effective date that provides adequate time for the waiver process to conclude.
336	
337	This summary is for internal reference purposes only and does not constitute legal advice to Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. or any other party. The summary is based on the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement dated March 12, 2021, as amended by the First Amendment dated September 8, 2022 and the Second Amendment dated June 15, 2023. Refer to the full Credit Agreement and all amendments thereto for the definitive and complete terms governing the senior secured revolving credit facility.
338
