The engagement followed the unsealing of a qui tam complaint originally filed under seal in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey in March 2021 by Dr. Anita Patel, a former Senior Medical Science Liaison at Greenvale who was employed by the Company from August 2018 through November 2020.
39	
40	The qui tam complaint was filed under the False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 et seq., and alleged violations of the Anti-Kickback Statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b, arising from Greenvale\'s nationwide speaker programs and healthcare provider consulting arrangements associated with two of the Company\'s branded pharmaceutical products: Neurovan, indicated for the treatment of epilepsy, and Cardivex, indicated for the treatment of atrial fibrillation. The complaint covered the period from January 2019 through December 2022 and alleged that the Company utilized these programs as vehicles for providing unlawful remuneration to high-prescribing physicians in exchange for prescribing and recommending Neurovan and Cardivex.
41	
42	The investigation was conducted over approximately eighteen months, from June 2021 through September 2022, when this report was initially prepared. Supplemental updates have been incorporated through December 2024 as the government\'s parallel investigation progressed, including following the service of a grand jury subpoena on Greenvale in March 2023. During the course of the investigation, we reviewed approximately 1.2 million documents collected from thirty-five custodians and conducted interviews of sixty-eight current and former employees of the Company, all pursuant to Upjohn warnings. The scope and methodology of the investigation are described in detail in Section II below.
43	
44	In summary, the investigation identified significant compliance deficiencies in the Company\'s speaker program operations and consulting fee arrangements during the 2019--2022 period. A subset of speaker events lacked legitimate educational purpose, exhibiting characteristics inconsistent with bona fide promotional speaker programs, including events with no substantive presentation, events where audiences consisted primarily of the speaker\'s own staff or family members, and events at high-end venues with no discernible educational content. Additionally, certain consulting fee arrangements were disproportionate to the services actually rendered, with a subset of physicians receiving substantial fees despite providing minimal or no documented consulting services.
45	
46	However, the investigation found that knowledge of the problematic practices was concentrated at the Regional Sales Director and Vice President of Medical Affairs level, not at the executive leadership level of the Company. The investigation\'s best estimate of improper speaker payments is \$11.1 million (within a range of \$9.8 million to \$12.4 million), which is materially lower than the government\'s asserted figure of \$14.3 million. Separately, the investigation estimates that approximately \$2.8 million of the \$6.2 million in consulting fees paid to healthcare providers during the relevant period were likely improper, bringing the total estimated improper payments to approximately \$13.9 million --- substantially below the government\'s aggregate figure of \$20.5 million.
47	
48	The investigation\'s findings diverge from the government\'s draft stipulated statement of facts in three material respects: (1) the scope of management knowledge of the alleged misconduct; (2) the quantum of improper payments; and (3) the characterization of corporate intent. These discrepancies are of critical importance as the Company approaches negotiations regarding the government\'s proposed Deferred Prosecution Agreement (\"DPA\"), which was presented in draft form in October 2024 with an anticipated execution date of February 1, 2025. DPA negotiations are scheduled for January 15, 2025. These discrepancies are detailed throughout this report and consolidated in Section XI for ease of reference.
49	
50	**[II. Scope and Methodology of Investigation]{.underline}**
51	
52	**II.A. Engagement and Authorization**
53	
54	Whitfield & Crane LLP was formally retained on June 15, 2021, pursuant to an engagement letter executed by Janet Huang, General Counsel of Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. The engagement followed preliminary consultations between Elena Vasquez, lead partner of Whitfield & Crane\'s white-collar defense and investigations practice group, and Ms. Huang during the first two weeks of June 2021, during which the scope and parameters of the investigation were discussed. Those preliminary discussions were conducted under the attorney-client privilege in anticipation of the formal engagement.
55	
56	The internal investigation was authorized by the Board of Directors of Greenvale through a resolution of the Audit Committee dated June 14, 2021. The Audit Committee directed that the investigation be conducted under the supervision of outside counsel and that findings be reported to the Audit Committee on a periodic basis, with interim updates provided as warranted by the pace of developments.
57	
58	The investigation was conducted under the direction and supervision of Elena Vasquez, who served as the lead partner responsible for all aspects of the engagement, supported by a team of partners, associates, forensic accountants, and document review attorneys at Whitfield & Crane. The primary purpose of the investigation was threefold: (1) to determine the facts and circumstances surrounding the allegations set forth in the qui tam complaint; (2) to assess the Company\'s potential legal exposure under the False Claims Act, the Anti-Kickback Statute, and related federal and state healthcare fraud statutes; and (3) to advise the Company on appropriate remedial measures to address any identified deficiencies in its compliance program and commercial operations. Throughout the investigation, all work was performed for the purpose of providing legal advice to the Company.
59	
60	**II.B. Document Review**
61	
62	The investigation team collected, processed, and reviewed approximately 1.2 million documents over the course of the investigation. The document collection encompassed a broad range of materials relevant to the Company\'s speaker program operations, consulting arrangements, and compliance activities during the period under review. Specifically, the collection included the following categories of documents:
63

65	>

Email collections covered the period from January 2018 through June 2022 to provide appropriate context preceding and following the core misconduct period.
69	>
70	> • **Compliance department records:** Internal compliance flags and exception reports generated by the compliance monitoring system, audit files and audit findings memoranda, compliance committee meeting minutes, compliance training records, and correspondence between compliance staff and the commercial organization regarding flagged events.
71	>
72	> • **Financial records:** Payment data from the accounts payable system, invoice records, wire transfer confirmations, and detailed ledger entries for all speaker honoraria and consulting fee payments made to healthcare providers during the relevant period.
73	>
74	> • **CRM data and prescription data reports:** Customer relationship management system records reflecting sales representative interactions with healthcare providers, together with third-party prescription data reports used by the commercial organization for territory management and targeting purposes.
75	
76	Document review was conducted using a technology-assisted review (\"TAR\") platform, which employed predictive coding algorithms to identify documents most likely to be relevant to the investigation\'s core issues. The TAR process was validated through iterative sampling and quality control measures. Supplemental manual review was conducted on approximately 85,000 documents that were identified as potentially relevant through the TAR process, keyword searches, and custodian-level prioritization. The manual review was performed by trained document review attorneys under the supervision of senior associates and partners at Whitfield & Crane.

78	**II.C. Witness Interviews**
79	
80	The investigation team conducted interviews of sixty-eight current and former employees of Greenvale over the course of the investigation. These interviews were designed to develop a comprehensive understanding of the Company\'s speaker program operations, consulting arrangements, compliance oversight, and the organizational dynamics that contributed to the identified deficiencies. The individuals interviewed included representatives from the following functional areas:
81	
82	**Executive leadership team:** Dr. Marcus Ellison, Chief Executive Officer; Janet Huang, General Counsel; Thomas Bridwell, Chief Financial Officer; and Patricia Knowles, Chief Compliance Officer. Each member of the executive team was interviewed at least once, with follow-up sessions as needed to address specific issues identified during the document review.
83	
84	**Commercial leadership:** Kevin Driscoll, Regional Sales Director for the Northeast Region; Maria Santos, Regional Sales Director for the Southeast Region; and other regional and district sales managers responsible for overseeing field sales operations in various geographic territories. These interviews focused on the speaker nomination process, sales force incentive structures, and the relationship between prescribing volume and speaker selection decisions.
85	
86	**Medical Affairs personnel:** Dr. Leonard Kwan, former Vice President of Medical Affairs, who departed Greenvale in March 2022 and was interviewed once through his personal counsel, Marcus Feldman of Hargrove & Rhodes LLP; medical science liaisons involved in clinical interactions with healthcare providers; and medical directors responsible for overseeing the medical review of speaker program content and consulting arrangements.

88	**Sales representatives:** Approximately thirty individuals from the field sales organization who were directly involved in coordinating speaker events, recruiting speakers, and managing relationships with healthcare providers in their territories. These interviews provided granular detail regarding day-to-day speaker program operations and the directives received from regional and district management.
89	
90	**Compliance department staff:** Approximately eight individuals, including compliance analysts responsible for monitoring speaker events, reviewing flagged events, and maintaining compliance records. These interviews addressed the compliance department\'s monitoring processes, escalation procedures, and resource constraints.
91	
92	**Finance and accounts payable personnel:** Approximately five individuals from the finance organization responsible for processing speaker honoraria payments and consulting fee disbursements.
93	
94	All interviews were conducted pursuant to Upjohn warnings, which were administered at the outset of each interview. Interviewees were advised that the investigation was being conducted by Whitfield & Crane on behalf of the Company; that the attorney-client privilege for the communications during the interview belonged to the Company, not to the individual; that the Company could choose to waive the privilege and disclose the contents of the interview to third parties, including the government; and that the individual was encouraged to answer questions truthfully and completely. Where interviewees were represented by personal counsel, coordination regarding the timing and scope of the interview was conducted with personal counsel.
95	
96	Dr. Anita Patel, the relator in the qui tam action, was not interviewed as part of this investigation. Dr. Patel had departed the Company in November 2020, prior to the formal engagement of Whitfield & Crane, and was represented in the qui tam action by Michael Greenberg of Stonebridge Hawkins LLP, 55 Hudson Yards, Suite 3400, New York, NY 10001. Given Dr. Patel\'s adverse posture and the pendency of the qui tam litigation, it was not appropriate to seek an interview directly.
97	
98	**II.D. Limitations.** The investigation was subject to certain limitations that should be considered in evaluating the findings presented in this report.
99	
100	First, several former employees declined to participate in voluntary interviews or were available only through their personal counsel, who in certain instances restricted the scope of questioning. Most notably, Dr. Leonard Kwan, the former Vice President of Medical Affairs and a central figure in the consulting fee arrangements, was interviewed only once through his personal counsel, Marcus Feldman of Hargrove & Rhodes LLP. Counsel for Dr. Kwan limited the scope of questions regarding certain topics, including Dr. Kwan\'s specific knowledge of the relationship between consulting fee payments and prescribing behavior, and his communications with the regional sales directors regarding consulting engagement nominations. As a result, the investigation\'s findings regarding Dr. Kwan\'s state of mind and the extent of his knowledge are based in part on documentary evidence rather than his direct testimony.
101	
102	Second, the investigation relied upon available documentary evidence and the recollections of witnesses. Given that certain of the events at issue occurred as early as 2019, the passage of time may have affected the quality and reliability of witness recollections, particularly with respect to conversations, meetings, and decisions that were not contemporaneously documented in writing.
103	
104	Third, the investigation did not have access to the government\'s evidence, the full scope of the government\'s witness interviews, or the complete qui tam complaint. Certain portions of the complaint remained under seal during the investigation period, and the government has not shared its complete investigative file or its methodology for calculating the asserted quantum of improper payments. Accordingly, the investigation\'s assessment of the government\'s position is based on information available from the unsealed portions of the complaint, communications with the USAO, and the government\'s draft DPA and stipulated facts.
105	
106	Finally, as with any internal investigation, this report reflects the investigation team\'s assessment of the evidence as of the date of this report. Additional information obtained by the government or by the Company after the date of this report may alter the factual record or the conclusions drawn from it.
107	
108	**[III. Background: Greenvale\'s Speaker Program and Consulting Arrangements]{.underline}**
109	
110	**III.A. Company Overview**
111	
112	Greenvale Pharmaceuticals, Inc. is a publicly traded specialty pharmaceutical company incorporated in the State of Delaware and headquartered at 400 Commerce Boulevard, Suite 1200, Princeton, New Jersey 08540. The Company\'s shares are listed on the NASDAQ Stock Market under the ticker symbol GVPH. For the fiscal year ending December 31, 2023, Greenvale reported total revenue of approximately \$2.84 billion and had a market capitalization of approximately \$6.1 billion.
113	
114	Greenvale\'s commercial portfolio consists of three branded pharmaceutical products: Neurovan, a branded anti-epileptic drug indicated for the treatment of partial-onset and generalized seizures in adult and pediatric patients; Cardivex, a branded antiarrhythmic agent indicated for the management of atrial fibrillation; and Osteorin, a branded bisphosphonate indicated for the treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. During the alleged misconduct period of 2019 through 2022, the combined revenues attributable to Neurovan and Cardivex --- the two products at issue in this investigation --- totaled approximately \$4.12 billion.
115	
116	Greenvale has a relevant prior enforcement history. In 2014, the Company entered into a Corporate Integrity Agreement (\"CIA\") with the Office of Inspector General (\"OIG\") of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in connection with a settlement of allegations relating to off-label promotion of Osteorin. The CIA imposed heightened compliance obligations for a five-year term and expired in 2019. As detailed elsewhere in this report, the expiration of the CIA coincided with a significant increase in speaker program activity and a relaxation of certain compliance controls that had been maintained during the CIA period. The Company\'s prior enforcement history is also relevant to the government\'s penalty calculation, as the draft DPA includes a recidivism multiplier attributable to the 2014 CIA.
117	
118	**III.B. The Speaker Program**
119	
120	Greenvale operated a nationwide speaker program for Neurovan and Cardivex, the stated purpose of which was to educate healthcare providers on the clinical use, safety profiles, and appropriate prescribing of these products. The program was designed to engage qualified physicians as paid speakers to deliver branded or unbranded clinical presentations to audiences of other healthcare providers, including physicians, physician assistants, nurse practitioners, and pharmacists, in group settings at restaurants, hotels, medical offices, or other venues.
121	
122	The speaker program was a significant component of the Company\'s commercial strategy. During the 2019--2022 period, approximately 4,200 speaker events were conducted per year across the Company\'s geographic footprint, with events spanning all major therapeutic markets and geographic regions. The total speaker honoraria paid by Greenvale during the 2019--2022 period was \$38.6 million, broken down by year as follows:
123	
124	 -----------------------------------------------------------------------
125	 **Fiscal Year** **Speaker Honoraria Paid**
126	 ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
127	 2019 \$8.4 million
128	
129	 2020 \$10.2 million
130	
131	 2021 \$11.1 million
132	
133	 2022 \$8.9 million
134	
135	 **Total (2019--2022)** **\$38.6 million**
136	 -----------------------------------------------------------------------
137	
138	The speaker program was managed operationally by the commercial organization, with primary responsibility residing in the field sales force under the supervision of regional and district sales directors. The Medical Affairs department played a nominal approval role, as speaker nominations originated from the field sales organization and were required to be approved by Medical Affairs prior to a physician being added to the approved speaker roster. According to Greenvale\'s written policies, speakers were to be selected based on clinical expertise, familiarity with the product\'s labeled indications, and demonstrated presentation ability. The policies expressly prohibited the selection of speakers based on prescribing volume or as a reward for prescribing the Company\'s products.
139	
140	In practice, as detailed in Section IV below, the investigation found that the speaker nomination and selection process did not consistently adhere to these policies, and that in certain regions, prescribing volume was a primary factor in speaker selection decisions.
141	
142	**III.C. The Consulting Fee Arrangements**
143	
144	Separately from the speaker program, Greenvale engaged healthcare providers as paid consultants for a variety of advisory and research-oriented activities related to Neurovan and Cardivex. These engagements were structured as advisory board participation, market research surveys, clinical input sessions, and ad hoc consulting arrangements on topics such as formulary strategy, patient identification, and clinical practice patterns.
145	
146	During the 2019--2022 period, forty-seven high-prescribing physicians received consulting fees from Greenvale, with total consulting payments during this period of \$6.2 million:
147	
148	 -----------------------------------------------------------------------
149	 **Fiscal Year** **Consulting Fees Paid**
150	 ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
151	 2019 \$1.1 million
152	
153	 2020 \$1.6 million
154	
155	 2021 \$1.9 million
156	
157	 2022 \$1.6 million
158	
159	 **Total (2019--2022)** **\$6.2 million**
160	 -----------------------------------------------------------------------
161	
162	The consulting fee arrangements were subject to the approval of Dr. Leonard Kwan, the then-Vice President of Medical Affairs, who had primary authority over the engagement of healthcare providers for consulting and advisory purposes. The advisory boards typically convened two to three times per year at hotel or restaurant venues, with individual consulting fees ranging from approximately \$5,000 to \$50,000 per physician per engagement, depending on the nature of the engagement and the physician\'s level of involvement. As detailed in Section V below, the investigation identified significant concerns regarding the documentation of services rendered, the proportionality of fees to work performed, and the approval process for these arrangements.
163	
164	**[IV. Findings: Speaker Program]{.underline}**
165	
166	**IV.A. Overview of Speaker Program Findings**
167	
168	The investigation identified a subset of speaker events during the 2019--2022 period that lacked legitimate educational purpose or exhibited characteristics inconsistent with bona fide promotional speaker programs operated in compliance with the Anti-Kickback Statute and applicable OIG guidance. These findings are significant and represent a material compliance failure.
169	
170	However, it is important to note at the outset that the majority of the approximately 16,800 total events conducted over the four-year period (approximately 4,200 events per year over four years) appeared to involve genuine educational presentations delivered to appropriate audiences by qualified speakers. The problematic events, while constituting a meaningful subset, do not represent the entirety of Greenvale\'s speaker program operations.
171	
172	The events identified as problematic by the investigation generally fell into three categories: (1) events at which no substantive clinical presentation was delivered, where the event appeared to consist solely of a meal or social gathering with no educational component; (2) events where the audience consisted primarily or entirely of the speaker\'s own office staff, family members, or other individuals who were not appropriate targets for clinical education regarding Neurovan or Cardivex; and (3) events held at high-end venues, such as upscale restaurants or entertainment establishments, where the setting was inconsistent with an educational purpose and where meal and entertainment costs significantly exceeded what would be expected for a bona fide educational program. Many of the most problematic events exhibited characteristics from more than one of these categories simultaneously.
173	
174	**IV.B. Quantification of Improper Speaker Payments**
175	
176	The investigation team developed a rigorous methodology for categorizing the approximately 16,800 speaker events conducted during the 2019--2022 period, with the objective of identifying those events that were potentially improper and quantifying the associated payments. Events were classified into three tiers based on the strength and nature of the evidence indicating impropriety.
177	
178	**Tier 1 --- Clearly Improper:** This category encompasses events with clear and unambiguous indicia of sham activity, where the documentary and testimonial evidence strongly supported a finding that the event lacked any legitimate educational purpose. Tier 1 events included events for which no attendee sign-in sheets could be located; events for which multiple witnesses confirmed that no clinical presentation was delivered; events where the attendee list consisted entirely of the speaker\'s own office staff (receptionists, billing clerks, medical assistants) with no clinicians in attendance; and events held at venues with no presentation capability (e.g., no screen, no projector, no private dining area) and no evidence that any presentation materials were distributed. The investigation identified approximately 620 events meeting the Tier 1 criteria over the four-year period, with associated speaker honoraria payments of approximately \$6.3 million. These events represent the clearest examples of payments that served no legitimate purpose and were, in substance, remuneration to physicians linked to their prescribing of Neurovan and Cardivex.
179	
180	**Tier 2 --- Likely Improper:** This category encompasses events with significant red flags suggesting that the event was not a bona fide educational program, though some limited indicia of legitimate activity were present. Tier 2 events included events where a presentation was delivered but was significantly abbreviated (e.g., presentations lasting five to ten minutes at events spanning two or more hours); events with very small audiences consisting primarily of repeat attendees who had attended numerous prior events on the same topic; events held at high-end restaurants where per-person meal costs significantly exceeded the Company\'s stated meal cost guidelines, and where the meal and social component of the event substantially dominated the educational component; and events where attendees were present but their qualifications to benefit from the clinical content were questionable. The investigation identified approximately 530 events in this category, with associated payments of approximately \$4.8 million. While these events had some characteristics of legitimate speaker programs, the overall pattern of activity was more consistent with a compensation mechanism for participating physicians than with a genuine educational initiative.
181	
182	**Tier 3 --- Potentially Improper:** This category encompasses events where concerns were identified but the evidence was ambiguous, such that a definitive determination of impropriety could not be made. Tier 3 events included events that were flagged by the compliance department but subsequently approved after internal review; events with adequate attendee counts but where questions existed about whether the attendees were appropriate targets for the presentation content; and events that were facially compliant with the Company\'s policies but where circumstantial evidence --- such as the speaker\'s prescribing patterns or the frequency of events in a particular territory --- raised concerns. Approximately 300 events fell into this category, with associated payments of approximately \$1.3 million. For these events, the evidence was insufficiently clear to support a definitive finding of impropriety, though the investigation team acknowledges that some of these events may, upon closer scrutiny or with additional evidence available to the government, prove to have been improper.
183	
184	Based on this tiered analysis, the investigation\'s **best estimate of improper speaker payments during the 2019--2022 period is \$11.1 million**, representing the sum of Tier 1 (\$6.3 million) and Tier 2 (\$4.8 million) events. The investigation established a **range of \$9.8 million to \$12.4 million** to account for classification uncertainty. The low end of the range (\$9.8 million) reflects a more conservative classification in which only the most egregious Tier 1 events and a subset of the stronger Tier 2 events are counted, excluding Tier 2 events where limited indicia of legitimate activity were more substantial. The high end of the range (\$12.4 million) includes all Tier 1 and Tier 2 events plus approximately \$1.3 million of Tier 3 events where the evidence, on balance, was more consistent with improper than proper activity.

Based on this tiered analysis, the investigation\'s **best estimate of improper speaker payments during the 2019--2022 period is \$11.1 million**, representing the sum of Tier 1 (\$6.3 million) and Tier 2 (\$4.8 million) events. The investigation established a **range of \$9.8 million to \$12.4 million** to account for classification uncertainty. The low end of the range (\$9.8 million) reflects a more conservative classification in which only the most egregious Tier 1 events and a subset of the stronger Tier 2 events are counted, excluding Tier 2 events where limited indicia of legitimate activity were more substantial. The high end of the range (\$12.4 million) includes all Tier 1 and Tier 2 events plus approximately \$1.3 million of Tier 3 events where the evidence, on balance, was more consistent with improper than proper activity.

This analysis yields a critical discrepancy with the government\'s position. The government alleges approximately \$14.3 million in improper speaker payments during the 2019--2022 period and characterizes this figure as a \"minimum,\" implying that the actual amount of improper payments may be higher still. The government\'s figure exceeds the investigation\'s best estimate by \$3.2 million (\$14.3 million minus \$11.1 million) and exceeds even the high end of the investigation\'s range by \$1.9 million (\$14.3 million minus \$12.4 million). Based on the investigation\'s analysis, the government\'s \$14.3 million figure appears to include substantially all Tier 3 events --- the very events that the investigation determined could not be definitively classified as improper --- and may also include some events that the investigation determined were legitimate based on the available evidence. The government has not shared its methodology for arriving at the \$14.3 million figure, nor has it provided the underlying data or classification criteria used in its analysis. The government\'s characterization of \$14.3 million as a \"minimum\" is particularly concerning, as it implies that the government\'s actual assessment of improper payments may extend even further, potentially encompassing events that the investigation found to be facially compliant.

This discrepancy is of material importance because the government\'s draft DPA employs the \$14.3 million figure as the baseline for the speaker payment component of the criminal penalty calculation. Combined with the government\'s treatment of the entire \$6.2 million in consulting fees as improper, the government arrives at a total alleged improper payment figure of \$20.5 million, which forms the basis for a criminal penalty of \$187.5 million. As discussed further in Section X, reductions in the baseline payment figure would translate directly into reductions in the penalty amount.

**IV.C. Directives from Regional Sales Leadership**

The investigation found that certain Regional Sales Directors actively encouraged field sales representatives to recruit high-prescribing physicians as speakers, in direct contravention of Greenvale\'s speaker program policies. The most direct evidence of this practice was found in the email communications of Kevin Driscoll, Regional Sales Director for the Northeast Region, and Maria Santos, Regional Sales Director for the Southeast Region.

Kevin Driscoll sent multiple email communications to his district managers and sales representatives instructing them to prioritize high-prescribing physicians when nominating speakers for the Neurovan and Cardivex speaker programs. In one illustrative email dated November 12, 2019, Driscoll wrote to his district managers: \"I need our top prescribers locked in as speakers for Q1. Don\'t worry about whether they\'re good presenters --- we\'ll work with them.\" This directive explicitly deprioritized presentation ability --- a core criterion under the Company\'s speaker selection policies --- in favor of prescribing volume. The implication of the message was unmistakable: physicians who wrote the most prescriptions for Greenvale\'s products should be offered speaking opportunities regardless of their qualifications as speakers. Additional emails from Driscoll during the 2019--2020 period reinforced this message, with Driscoll tracking prescribing data alongside speaker engagement metrics and directing his team to \"fill the speaker roster\" with physicians who demonstrated the highest prescribing loyalty to Neurovan and Cardivex.

Maria Santos sent similar directives within the Southeast Region. In an email dated January 8, 2020, Santos instructed her team: \"For Q2 planning, prioritize getting our champions on the speaker roster. If they\'re writing scrips, they should be getting programs.\" Like Driscoll\'s communications, Santos\'s directive made prescribing volume the primary criterion for speaker selection, inverting the policy framework that required speakers to be chosen based on their clinical expertise and communication abilities. Santos also maintained an informal tracking spreadsheet that correlated individual physician prescribing data with speaker engagement frequency, which the investigation identified in the document review and which Santos acknowledged during her interview.

Both Driscoll and Santos were interviewed by the investigation team. Each acknowledged that they had prioritized prescribing volume as a factor in speaker selection recommendations. However, both characterized this practice as consistent with standard industry practice rather than improper conduct. Driscoll stated that \"every company identifies high prescribers for their speaker programs --- it\'s how you ensure the speakers have real-world experience with the product.\" Santos offered a similar characterization, stating that \"our best speakers are the ones who use the product every day.\" The investigation team notes that while familiarity with a product is a legitimate factor in speaker selection, the emails reviewed indicate that Driscoll and Santos elevated prescribing volume above all other selection criteria, including presentation skills and clinical expertise, and that the purpose of their directives was to use speaker program compensation as an inducement to maintain and increase prescribing behavior.

These directives were inconsistent with Greenvale\'s written speaker program policies, which explicitly stated that speakers were to be selected based on \"clinical expertise, familiarity with the therapeutic area, and the ability to deliver effective educational presentations.\" The policies further stated that \"prescribing history should not be the primary basis for speaker selection.\" The gap between written policy and actual practice, as directed by regional leadership, is a central finding of this investigation.

**IV.D. Compliance Department Review of Flagged Events**

Greenvale\'s compliance department maintained a monitoring system designed to identify potentially problematic speaker events based on certain automated and manual triggers, including events with very low attendee counts, events at high-cost venues, events involving speakers who appeared on the program with unusually high frequency, and events flagged by individual compliance analysts based on their review of event documentation. During the 2019--2022 period, the compliance department flagged a total of 312 speaker events as potentially problematic.

Of these 312 flagged events, only 41 --- approximately 13% --- were actually cancelled prior to or after the event. The cancellations generally involved the most egregious cases, such as events where the speaker had been permanently removed from the speaker roster or events where venue arrangements had been made at obviously inappropriate locations. The remaining 271 flagged events proceeded after what the investigation found to be cursory and inadequate review.

The review process for flagged events typically consisted of a single email exchange between the compliance analyst who flagged the event and the responsible sales manager or district manager. In the typical pattern, the compliance analyst would send a brief inquiry noting the flag --- e.g., \"This event has been flagged due to low attendee count. Please provide justification.\" --- and the sales manager would respond with a one- to two-sentence justification, such as \"The attendees are all relevant prescribers in the area. The event is appropriate.\" The compliance analyst would then close the flag and the event would proceed. The investigation found no instances in which a compliance analyst conducted any independent verification of the sales manager\'s justification, requested supporting documentation, or followed up on events that proceeded after the initial review.

More significantly, the investigation found no evidence that any of the 312 flagged events were escalated beyond the compliance analyst level to senior management, the General Counsel, or the Audit Committee. The compliance department operated in a largely autonomous fashion with respect to individual event reviews, without a formal escalation protocol requiring that events meeting certain severity thresholds be reported to the CCO, the General Counsel, or the Board. This lack of escalation meant that the recurring patterns of potentially problematic speaker events --- which were visible in the aggregate data, if not always at the individual event level --- were never brought to the attention of senior decision-makers who might have intervened.

Patricia Knowles, the Chief Compliance Officer, addressed this issue during her interview. Knowles stated that she was generally aware that her compliance team flagged speaker events and that a review process was in place, but that she relied on her compliance analysts to handle event-level reviews and did not independently scrutinize individual flagged events. She acknowledged that the compliance department lacked the resources and, critically, the organizational authority to conduct robust independent reviews of individual events or to unilaterally cancel events that the commercial organization had determined should proceed. Knowles noted that when her analysts raised concerns about events that had been approved to proceed, they were sometimes met with pushback from the sales organization, and that the compliance department did not have a clear mandate to override commercial decisions absent escalation to senior management --- an escalation path that, as noted above, was not effectively utilized.

**[V. Findings: Consulting Fee Arrangements]{.underline}**

**V.A. Overview.** The investigation examined the consulting fee arrangements maintained between Greenvale and forty-seven high-prescribing physicians who received a combined \$6.2 million in consulting fees during the 2019--2022 period. These consulting engagements were structured as advisory board participation, market research surveys, and clinical input sessions related to Neurovan and Cardivex. The engagements were nominally designed to obtain physician insights on topics such as product positioning, clinical practice patterns, formulary dynamics, and emerging treatment paradigms in the epilepsy and atrial fibrillation therapeutic areas.

Dr. Leonard Kwan, then-Vice President of Medical Affairs, had primary approval authority over all consulting arrangements with healthcare providers. Kwan was responsible for reviewing and approving consulting agreements, determining the scope of work for each engagement, and authorizing the associated fee amounts. The investigation\'s findings regarding these arrangements are set forth below.

**V.B. Assessment of Fair Market Value**

In order to assess whether the consulting fees paid to the forty-seven physicians were consistent with fair market value (\"FMV\") for the services actually rendered, the investigation team retained an independent healthcare valuation consultant with expertise in physician compensation benchmarking and FMV analysis for healthcare provider consulting arrangements. The valuation consultant reviewed the consulting agreements, scope-of-work documents, deliverables (where available), advisory board meeting records, and fee schedules for each of the forty-seven physicians, and compared the fees paid against established FMV benchmarks for comparable consulting services in the pharmaceutical industry.

The valuation analysis yielded the following findings:

For approximately fifteen of the forty-seven physicians, the fees paid were within the range of FMV benchmarks for comparable consulting services. These engagements were generally supported by documented scopes of work, evidence of substantive participation in advisory board discussions, and deliverables that were commensurate with the fees paid. While these arrangements are not entirely free from regulatory risk --- given the physicians\' prescribing profiles --- the investigation found no basis to characterize them as improper.

For approximately twenty physicians, the fees paid exceeded FMV benchmarks by 25% to 75%, suggesting that the fees were disproportionate to the scope and duration of services actually rendered. In many of these cases, the scope-of-work documents described broad consulting responsibilities, but the actual work performed --- as reflected in meeting attendance records, deliverables, and physician-generated work product --- was substantially less than what the fees would suggest. For example, several physicians were paid \$25,000 to \$40,000 for participation in a single advisory board meeting lasting approximately three to four hours, when comparable FMV benchmarks would support fees in the range of \$10,000 to \$20,000 for such participation. While these arrangements involved some legitimate consulting activity, the excess fees create significant risk under the Anti-Kickback Statute.

For approximately twelve physicians, the investigation identified minimal or no documentation that the physicians had provided any substantive consulting services, despite receiving fees ranging from \$15,000 to \$50,000 per engagement. In several instances, the purported \"advisory board\" meetings consisted of a dinner at an upscale restaurant with no formal agenda, no presentation materials distributed to participants, no documented discussion topics, and no written takeaways or deliverables generated from the meeting. For these engagements, the investigation could not identify any legitimate consulting work product that corresponded to the fees paid. The total fees paid to these twelve physicians during the 2019--2022 period was approximately \$2.8 million.

The investigation concluded that the consulting fee arrangements with these twelve physicians were likely improper under the Anti-Kickback Statute, as the payments appeared designed to reward prescribing behavior and to maintain the physicians\' loyalty to Neurovan and Cardivex, rather than to compensate for legitimate consulting services rendered. The remaining consulting arrangements --- involving approximately \$3.4 million in payments to the other thirty-five physicians --- involved varying degrees of documentation deficiency but had at least some indicia of legitimate consulting activity. The investigation was unable to conclude that these payments were clearly improper, though several fall within a gray area that presents regulatory risk.

It should be noted that the government\'s position treats the entire \$6.2 million in consulting fees as improper. The investigation\'s findings support a significantly narrower characterization, with the strongest evidence of impropriety focused on the approximately \$2.8 million paid to the twelve physicians for whom no meaningful consulting services were documented.

**V.C. Role of Dr. Leonard Kwan**

Dr. Leonard Kwan, as Vice President of Medical Affairs, had final approval authority over all consulting fee arrangements with healthcare providers. In this capacity, Kwan was the gatekeeper for the engagement of physicians as paid consultants and for the authorization of consulting fees. The investigation examined Kwan\'s role in the approval process and the extent of his knowledge regarding the nature of the consulting arrangements.

The investigation found that Dr. Kwan approved consulting engagements with limited scrutiny. In multiple documented instances, Kwan signed off on consulting agreements and fee authorizations based solely on the recommendation of the regional sales directors --- the same individuals who were responsible for identifying and nominating speakers for the speaker program --- without independently verifying the scope of work to be performed, the physician\'s qualifications for the specific consulting task, or whether the fees proposed were consistent with FMV benchmarks. Kwan\'s approval process appeared to be largely perfunctory, consisting of a signature on a pre-prepared approval form with minimal or no notation of independent review.

The documentary record includes email chains in which regional sales directors recommended specific physicians for consulting engagements, often citing the physician\'s \"strong relationship\" with Greenvale products or \"significant territory influence,\" language that is more consistent with a prescribing-based rationale than a qualifications-based rationale. Kwan approved these recommendations without questioning the basis for the selection or requesting additional information about the physician\'s qualifications for the consulting work described in the scope of work.

Dr. Kwan departed Greenvale in March 2022. His departure was characterized internally by the Company as a voluntary resignation, though the timing --- approximately nine months after the unsealing of the qui tam complaint and the commencement of this investigation --- is notable. In his interview, which was conducted through his personal counsel, Kwan stated that he believed the consulting arrangements were legitimate and within industry norms. He maintained that the advisory boards served a genuine business purpose and that the fees paid were appropriate for the level of expertise the physicians brought to the engagements. However, as noted in Section II.D, Kwan\'s counsel limited the scope of questions on certain topics, and the investigation was unable to fully explore Kwan\'s understanding of the relationship between consulting fees and prescribing behavior.

The investigation found no evidence that Dr. Kwan personally benefited from the consulting arrangements beyond his normal compensation from the Company. There was no indication that Kwan received any portion of the consulting fees, had a personal financial relationship with any of the consulting physicians, or was motivated by personal financial gain. Dr. Kwan was the most senior individual with direct involvement in approving the consulting arrangements, and his role is central to the investigation\'s assessment of the management level at which knowledge of the problematic practices resided.

**[VI. Findings: Scope of Management Knowledge]{.underline}**

**VI.A. Knowledge at the Regional Sales Director and VP Level**

A critical question for purposes of the government\'s DPA negotiations and the draft stipulated facts is the organizational level at which knowledge of the problematic speaker program and consulting fee practices resided. The investigation examined this question extensively, drawing on documentary evidence, interview testimony, and analysis of the organizational structure and communication flows within the Company.

The investigation found that awareness of the problematic practices was concentrated at two organizational levels:

**Regional Sales Director level:** Kevin Driscoll (Regional Sales Director, Northeast Region) and Maria Santos (Regional Sales Director, Southeast Region) had direct knowledge of, and actively promoted, the use of the speaker program to reward high-prescribing physicians. Their email communications, described in detail in Section IV.C above, constitute direct documentary evidence of intent to use the speaker program as an inducement mechanism. These emails were sent to district managers and, in some cases, to individual sales representatives, and they explicitly directed the recruitment of physicians to the speaker program based on prescribing volume rather than clinical expertise or presentation ability. The investigation also found that other regional sales directors not specifically named in this report were aware of similar practices in their respective regions, though the documentary evidence of their involvement was less direct than in the cases of Driscoll and Santos. In the aggregate, the evidence indicates that the use of prescribing volume as a primary driver of speaker selection was a widespread practice at the regional sales director level.

**VP of Medical Affairs level:** Dr. Leonard Kwan approved consulting arrangements with minimal oversight and was aware, based on the documentation reviewed, that certain consulting engagements lacked substantive deliverables or formal meeting structures. However, the investigation could not conclusively determine whether Kwan understood the arrangements to be improper under the Anti-Kickback Statute or whether he genuinely believed they were within acceptable parameters for physician consulting engagements. The documentary evidence shows a pattern of perfunctory approvals, but the investigation did not identify any communications from Kwan that explicitly acknowledged the use of consulting fees as inducements to prescribe.

No evidence was found that any individual above the VP level --- including members of the executive leadership team --- had actual knowledge that the speaker program or consulting arrangements were being used as inducements for prescribing behavior. The investigation\'s findings on executive leadership awareness are addressed in detail in the following section.

**VI.B. Executive Leadership Awareness**

The investigation specifically examined whether members of the executive leadership team were aware of the alleged misconduct. This question is of paramount importance because the government\'s draft stipulated statement of facts asserts that \"senior management, including members of the executive team, were aware of and tacitly approved the use of speaker programs as a vehicle for rewarding high-prescribing physicians.\" The investigation found no evidence supporting this characterization.

**Dr. Marcus Ellison (Chief Executive Officer):** Dr. Ellison was aware at a general level that Greenvale operated speaker programs and consulting arrangements for Neurovan and Cardivex, as these programs were discussed at a high level in quarterly business reviews and annual operating plan presentations. However, the investigation found no evidence that Ellison was informed of specific concerns about sham events, problematic speaker selection criteria, or disproportionate consulting fees. Ellison was not copied on any of the Driscoll or Santos emails directing speaker recruitment based on prescribing volume, nor was he included in any communications regarding specific flagged events or compliance concerns about the programs. In his interview, Ellison stated that he understood the speaker program and consulting arrangements to be standard commercial practices overseen by the compliance department, and that he was not aware of any concerns about the legitimacy of these activities until the qui tam complaint was unsealed in June 2021. The investigation found no evidence contradicting Ellison\'s account.

**Janet Huang (General Counsel):** Ms. Huang became aware of compliance concerns regarding the speaker program only after the qui tam complaint was unsealed in June 2021, at which time she promptly initiated the engagement of Whitfield & Crane to conduct this investigation. Prior to the unsealing, the investigation found no communications alerting Huang to specific concerns about the speaker program or consulting arrangements. Huang did not receive copies of compliance flags or exception reports related to speaker events, nor did the compliance department\'s reporting structure route such information through the legal department. Huang stated in her interview that she had no knowledge of the specific practices described in the qui tam complaint prior to its unsealing.

**Thomas Bridwell (Chief Financial Officer):** Mr. Bridwell approved the overall speaker program and consulting budgets as part of the annual operating plan process, which aggregated program expenditures at a high level. However, Bridwell had no visibility into individual speaker events, individual consulting engagements, or specific payment amounts to individual physicians. The financial approval process at the CFO level addressed total program budgets (e.g., \"Speaker Program --- Neurovan: \$5.2M\") rather than individual transactions. The investigation found no evidence that Bridwell was aware of any concerns about the legitimacy of specific payments within these programs, or that he received any communications flagging potential compliance issues with the speaker program or consulting arrangements.

**Patricia Knowles (Chief Compliance Officer):** Ms. Knowles occupied a somewhat different position from the other executive team members, as the compliance function reported to her and she had a broader responsibility for overseeing the Company\'s compliance program. Knowles was aware that her compliance team flagged speaker events through the monitoring system and that the majority of flagged events proceeded after review. However, Knowles stated in her interview that she relied on her compliance analysts\' assessments and did not independently review individual flagged events. She was not informed of the specific nature, volume, or patterns of the concerns identified through the flagging process until the qui tam complaint surfaced. While Knowles\'s level of awareness was greater than that of Ellison, Huang, or Bridwell, the investigation did not find evidence that Knowles had actual knowledge that the speaker program or consulting arrangements were being used as inducements.

**Conclusion on executive knowledge:** The investigation found no evidence that any member of the executive leadership team had actual knowledge of the improper nature of the speaker program practices or consulting fee arrangements identified in this report. At most, certain executives may have had constructive knowledge in the sense that they were aware of the existence of the programs, the general regulatory environment in which those programs operated, and the inherent risk associated with pharmaceutical speaker programs and HCP payments. However, constructive knowledge of general risk is qualitatively different from --- and falls far short of --- the government\'s characterization that \"senior management, including members of the executive team, were aware of and tacitly approved\" the specific conduct at issue.

The government\'s language in the draft stipulated facts is particularly problematic for three reasons. First, executive knowledge bears directly on the mens rea element of the Anti-Kickback Statute, which requires that a violation be committed \"knowingly and willfully.\" Stipulating to executive-level awareness would significantly strengthen any future criminal prosecution in the event of a DPA breach, by establishing that the Company\'s most senior leaders were aware of and acquiesced in the illegal conduct. Second, the stipulated facts would be available as admissions in parallel civil litigation, including potential shareholder derivative actions under state corporate law, securities fraud claims under Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and the ongoing False Claims Act proceedings. A stipulation that executive management was aware of and ap
